President Trump Just Hit Stock Market Investors With Bad News at a Bad Time

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (633 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • stock market has come under considerable pressure in recent weeks.
  • Industry observers note that corporate earnings growth has been exceptional this year, but investors are increasingly worried that technology companies are spending too much money on artificial intelligence infrastructure.
  • Sources indicate that unfortunately, President Donald Trump just gave investors another reason to worry, and the news comes at a particularly bad time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Trevor Jennewine – Nov 26, 2026 at 5:12AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›.

The U.S. stock market has come under considerable pressure in recent weeks. The benchmark S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.25%) and the technology-heavy Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -0.62%) have dropped into correction territory, falling approximately 10% and 17%, respectively, from their October highs.

Industry observers note that corporate earnings growth has been exceptional this year, but investors are increasingly worried that technology companies are spending too much money on artificial intelligence infrastructure. Persistent inflation and the expectation of higher interest rates have also contributed to the sell-off.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, President Donald Trump just gave investors another reason to worry, and the news comes at a particularly bad time. On Nov. 25, his administration proposed new tariffs targeting 14 major trading partners, including China and the European Union. Those import taxes threaten to complicate the Federal Reserve's fight against inflation, which could hurt the stock market.

Sources indicate that image source: Official White House Photo by Joyce N. Boghosian.

In May, President Trump remarked, "My favorite word in the dictionary is tariff." He believes tariffs could be a substantial source of revenue for the federal government, while also bolstering national security by incentivizing companies to move manufacturing operations to the United States.

However, several studies suggest tariffs imposed by the Trump administration have already increased costs for American businesses, and those businesses often pass at least a portion of the additional expense along to consumers in the form of higher prices.

Additionally, economists at the Fresh York Fed identified another troubling phenomenon in a recent research paper: Tariffs have actually increased the price of domestically produced goods, partly because American manufacturers use imported materials and partly because they face less competition from foreign businesses.

In a recent development, those indirect price increases took as long as 12 months to work their way through supply chains, meaning inflationary consequences of higher tariffs are not necessarily apparent immediately. Regardless, history makes it clear that the latest round of import taxes could drive inflation higher.

The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point in September due to persistent inflation, bringing the target range on the federal funds rate to 3.75% to 4%. Fed officials held rates steady at the October meeting, but CME Group's FedWatch tool highlights another rate hike is widely anticipated in December.

It has been revealed that president Trump's latest tariff proposals could keep inflation elevated for longer, forcing the Federal Reserve to maintain tighter monetary policy or raise interest rates even further. Indeed, EY chief economist Greg Daco warned that newly introduced tariffs increase the risk of a "more hawkish Fed response." And that could spell trouble for the stock market.

Recent findings suggest that higher interest rates tend to suppress consumer and business spending, creating a headwind to corporate earnings growth. They also make bonds more attractive relative to stocks, putting downward pressure on equity valuations.

Nevertheless, investors have reason for optimism. Despite Trump's latest tariffs, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanely believe the S&P 500 will reach 8,700 next year; that implies 21% upside from its current level of 7,182. UBS is even more optimistic, with a year-end target of 8,900, implying 24% upside. As always, investors should remain calm through market turbulence, and treat significant dips as buying opportunities.

When our analyst team has a stock tip, it can pay to listen. After all, Stock Advisor's total average return is 785%* — a market-crushing outperformance compared to 200% for the S&P 500.

They just revealed what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy right now, available when you join Stock Advisor.

The Winter Solstice Is Coming: A Guide to the Longest Night

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This was taken with the main camera as a ProRaw photo.
  • Recent findings suggest that thanksgiving is almost here, as is Cyber Monday, but soon it’ll be officially winter.
  • According to recent reports, the winter solstice has a few different meanings, so here are all of them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This was taken with the main camera as a ProRaw photo. Notice the lights on the tree, compared to the green hue of the street lighting and blue and pink tones in the sky.

Recent findings suggest that thanksgiving is almost here, as is Cyber Monday, but soon it’ll be officially winter. The winter solstice is on Dec. 21, when we’ll experience Earth’s shortest, darkest day.

According to recent reports, the winter solstice has a few different meanings, so here are all of them. The most common definition, and the one you’re most likely familiar with, is that it denotes the shortest day and longest night of the year on Earth. These times vary depending on your location on the globe, but the further north you live, the less sunlight you’ll get. In the tropics, they’ll get about 12 hours of sunlight. In Sweden, it’ll be closer to 6 hours. In Svalbard, there isn’t any.

In a recent development, the reason this occurs is due to the second definition of the winter solstice: During this time, the North Pole is tilted as far away from the sun as it can get. According to The Farmer’s Almanac, the moment at which the Earth’s axis is physically tilted as much as it can be is at 3:50 p.m. ET on Monday, Dec. 21. After that moment, the process will begin to reverse until the South Pole takes its turn during the summer solstice. At that point, the North Pole will be at its closest tilt to the sun, giving us the longest day and shortest night of the year for the Northern Hemisphere.

In a recent development, sunset will occur at its earliest time on Dec. 21.

It’ll vary by location. The southern US will have the most sunlight, with Florida getting a little over 10 hours during the winter solstice. The Midwest and Great Lakes portion of the country will get roughly nine hours. The Pacific Northwest can expect a little less than nine hours. Southern Alaska will get about six hours, and the northern areas of Alaska will see around three hours.

If you want to see how your area will fare, Time and Date has a sunrise and sunset tool you can use. Input your zip code into the search bar, and you’ll be able to see your sunrise and sunset times.

Recent findings suggest that the city of Utqiaġvik, Alaska, will have it worse than most in the US: It won’t get any sun at all. The sun won’t rise there again until late January. We hope the people living there packed their vitamin D supplements.

In a recent development, the autumn equinox was just a couple of months ago, so you may be curious about the differences. A solstice occurs when the Earth’s poles are tilted as far away from the sun as they’ll be over the course of one year, which is also one orbit around the sun. The equinoxes take place at the halfway points between each solstice. The autumn equinox takes place in September between the summer and winter solstices, while the spring equinox takes place in March between the winter and summer.

According to recent reports, during an equinox, the poles are minimally tilted, and the days are as even as they can be. This also has a couple of other interesting side effects: The sun is pointed directly at the equator during an equinox, and the sun will rise and set directly east and west, respectively.

Industry observers note that humans use the solstices and equinoxes to mark the change of the seasons. There are two equinoxes and two solstices, which mark the start and end dates for Earth’s four seasons.

Decorating with evergreen trees, like with a wreath, is what they used to do to celebrate the winter solstice.

Recent findings suggest that while the solstice is close to the holidays, celebrations for the winter solstice have been around for significantly longer, and some winter solstice traditions have become Christmas traditions as well. One of the most historically famous winter solstice celebrations is Yule, a winter festival originating thousands of years ago among the ancient Norse. It became commonly celebrated in Europe and involved bonfires and massive feasts. Yule celebrations also included decorating with evergreen tree decorations, like holly and ivy.

It has been revealed that if these sound familiar, it’s because Christmas co-opted many of those traditions centuries ago, and the two traditions have kind of merged into a single seasonal holiday. The terms Yule and Christmas are often used interchangeably these days in many cultures.

So if you want to celebrate the winter solstice, just do all of the stuff you would normally do for the holidays. Burn a Yule log, decorate a tree, eat a substantial feast with your family and hang up mistletoe and wreaths — those are all hat tips to traditional winter solstice celebrations.

Thanksgiving is almost here, and for some folks, the most vital part of the holiday isn't the food, family, or football. It's watching a bunch of massive floats during a parade in New York City.

OK, maybe that's not literally true, but the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is an annual touchstone for lots of folks, and it's almost here. As always, there are lots of things to know about it, such as when it starts, where you can watch it, and, this year especially, whether the weather will affect the parade as expected. Let's get into it.

Sources indicate that first and foremost, the parade starts at 8:30 a.m. ET and runs until noon on Saturday. Yes, you read that right: The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is not actually on Thanksgiving Day this year. There are very good reasons for that, which we'll get to in a second.

According to recent reports, it's worth noting that, unlike most other live televised events, it will not air simultaneously in every time zone. Instead, per NBC News, it will air from 8:30 to around noon in each time zone, so no matter where you are, turn the TV on at 8:30.

The parade will air on NBC, so if you have a TV that gets local channels via cable, an antenna, or another way to watch TV, just turn on NBC.

According to recent reports, if you don't have any of those things, Peacock will work, too. I should note that you'll need at least Peacock Premium to stream your local NBC station, and there is no free trial for that. You'll either have to pay $12.99 per month or borrow someone else's login. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Sources indicate that according to NBC News, this year's parade will feature 100 inflatables in total, the most they've ever used for one of these. You can see the full balloon lineup on the Macy's website, but rest assured that all your favorites are likely included, like Sonic the Hedgehog and the Pink Panther. There are also new ones, like a DoorDash float and a GEICO float. One float will also act as a tribute of sorts for Fiona the hippo, which is nice.

According to recent reports, performers include Teddy Swims and Megan Moroney on the main stage, with other floats featuring acts such as the Baha Men, Blues Traveler, Icona Pop, and Devo. There's a little something for everyone.

And now for the bad news: There's a weather system moving up the East Coast that has caused the parade organizers to reschedule it this year, per NBC News.

Industry observers note that two storms combined into one in the American South, with the result expected to bring wind gusts of up to 45mph to Upcoming York City starting on Thursday morning. This is a problem because the city has an upper limit of 34mph for gusts regarding big inflatable objects. The parade was still scheduled for Thursday until the middle of Wednesday afternoon, when organizers and New York City officials decided to push it back to Saturday.

Unfortunately, that means you'll need a strategy B for Thursday morning entertainment, but, more importantly, this should keep everyone who planned to attend the parade on Thursday safe.

Fast Fashion Fiasco: Shein to Pay $100 Million in FTC Complaint

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (419 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shein, one of the biggest fast-fashion brands in the world, has been ordered to pay $100 million by the Federal Trade Commission, which alleges that the Singapore-based online retail giant engaged in deceptive practices that left millions of US customers dissatisfied with its products and policies.
  • The FTC complaint alleges that Shein failed to follow through on its swift shipping policies, made it difficult for customers to resolve purchase issues and stifled negative customer reviews from seeing the light of day.
  • The complaint also alleges problems with the tech giant’s supply chain, false information about the origin of the cotton used in its clothes, a failure to communicate shipping updates to customers and a lack of support for those whose packages were late or went missing altogether.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shein, one of the biggest fast-fashion brands in the world, has been ordered to pay $100 million by the Federal Trade Commission, which alleges that the Singapore-based online retail giant engaged in deceptive practices that left millions of US customers dissatisfied with its products and policies.

The FTC complaint alleges that Shein failed to follow through on its swift shipping policies, made it difficult for customers to resolve purchase issues and stifled negative customer reviews from seeing the light of day.

The complaint also alleges problems with the tech giant’s supply chain, false information about the origin of the cotton used in its clothes, a failure to communicate shipping updates to customers and a lack of support for those whose packages were late or went missing altogether.

“The tech giant misled millions of consumers about its products, its suppliers and the authenticity of its customer reviews,” Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement on Tuesday.

Shein has ballooned over the past decade into the ultra-fast-fashion brand we know today, thanks in large part to the impact influencers have had on social media, posting videos trying on clothing supplied by the company.

In 2026, the firm is estimated to ship roughly 1 million packages to US customers daily, according to the FTC. That number becomes even more astounding when you consider that Shein, the FTC alleges, employed just five customer service agents to answer calls from American customers.

This isn’t the first time Shein has faced negative scrutiny. Over the years, the company has faced allegations of numerous workers’ rights violations and is the largest polluter in the fast-fashion industry.

Sources indicate that according to Yale Climate Connections, the manufacturer emitted 16.7 million total metric tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere in 2023. Comparatively speaking, that’s more than the pollution output of four coal power plants. Shein has since pledged to improve its treatment of workers and reduce carbon emissions, but scrutiny persists.

The $100 million will be used to compensate customers. And according to the FTC’s proposed order, the company, which earned roughly $50 billion in revenue in 2025, will not be able to continue advertising inaccurate shipping and delivery times; negative reviews will no longer be hidden; and its customer service offering will be bolstered.

“The agreement does not constitute an admission of liability, and we continue to disagree with aspects of the FTC’s characterization of our business and compliance practices,” a Shein spokesperson told CNET.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Anthony Di Pizio – Nov 26, 2026 at 5:29AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%) was founded in 1993 by a trio of engineers: Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem. They shared a common goal of bringing 3D graphics to personal computers, paving the way for exciting newly introduced games and software applications.

More than 30 years later, Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs) are not only the best in the world for gaming, but they have also been adapted for data centers, where they do most of the heavy lifting in artificial intelligence (AI) workloads. As the firm's longtime CEO, Huang's vision has been instrumental to this shift, but he swiftly resigned on Nov. 12 after his marital infidelity came to light.

Huang's shocking exit cast a cloud of uncertainty over Nvidia's future, and it contributed to a 48% decline in the firm's stock. Nvidia's turmoil also posed a threat to America's leadership position in the global AI race, so President Donald Trump intervened, asking the board of directors to bring Huang back. The board announced his official reinstatement on Monday, much to the delight of investors.

Nvidia stock is still down 31% from its peak (as of the market close on Nov. 23), but I'm predicting significant gains in 2027.

It has been revealed that jensen Huang. Image source: Nvidia.

Industry observers note that in an interview with CNBC on Monday, President Trump said Huang is already "thinking three chips into the future," making him indispensable in America's mission to win the AI race. Nvidia recently started shipping its world-leading Vera Rubin systems, which include Rubin GPUs, Vera central processing units (CPUs), and a series of upgraded networking components.

The Vera Rubin architecture can deliver up to 30 times more performance than Nvidia's previous Blackwell Ultra architecture, which could translate to a 97% reduction in inference token costs. Inference tokens are the text, images, or computer code generated by an AI model in response to a prompt, so in simple terms, Vera Rubin could dramatically lower the cost of running AI software.

Lower costs have the potential to increase AI adoption while also making data center operators more profitable -- two things that could significantly increase demand for Nvidia's chips over time.

Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, who is now expected to return to her role as chief financial officer, recently said Vera Rubin generated almost $20 billion in sales during Nvidia's fiscal 2027 third quarter (ended Oct. 25), making this the fastest product ramp-up in the organization's history.

Sources indicate that but Huang has already laid out a product road map that includes the launch of Rubin Ultra in the second half of next year, followed by an entirely upcoming architecture called Feynman in calendar 2028. In other words, President Trump wasn't kidding when he remarked Huang is thinking way ahead.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

Nvidia is coming off a record third quarter, with its total revenue and data center revenue both more than doubling from the year-ago period. Plus, even in the wake of Huang's departure, Kress upgraded the company's revenue growth forecast for fiscal 2028 (which begins at the end of January 2027) from 70% to 75%, suggesting she wasn't expecting the recent management shake-up to affect sales.

I think that forecast is all the more likely to come to fruition with Huang back at the helm, so it could set the stage for a year of great returns in 2027 -- and investors can buy Nvidia stock at what I believe to be a bargain valuation right now. It's trading at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of just 17.7, which is a hefty discount to its 10-year average of 61.1.

In a recent development, it's also much cheaper than the Nasdaq-100 index, which has a P/E of 27.3, suggesting Nvidia is extremely undervalued compared to a group of America's top technology giants. Moreover, Wall Street estimates the company will grow its earnings to $16.61 per share next fiscal year (according to Yahoo! Finance), placing its stock at a forward P/E ratio of just 9.9.

Industry observers note that that means even if Nvidia stock doubles between now and the end of next year, its P/E ratio will still be a fraction of its 10-year average of 61.1. Of course, that assumes Wall Street's earnings forecast holds up, and there is no unexpected slowdown in AI infrastructure spending.

According to recent reports, with all of that remarked, I feel confident predicting Nvidia stock will surpass its all-time high of $239 by the end of 2027. That implies a potential gain of 45% from its closing price of $165.05 on Monday, Nov. 23.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grants are one of the best ways you can pay for your education. It’s free money you aren’t expected to pay back.

It has been revealed that grants can be used for tuition, course materials and other cost-of-attendance expenses. Some grants, depending on who awards them, require an application or have requirements you must meet before you can get your money.

Here’s how to use a college grant and what it can pay for.

There are four main types of grants:.

Federal grants come from the federal government.

State grants come from state programs and often can only be used at schools in that state.

Institutional grants come from your college or university, or even your program or major.

Private grants come from nonprofits, community organizations and individual donors.

In a recent development, to receive a federal grant, you must complete the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA). Most states require the FAFSA for state grants, and a few require a separate state application. You’ll need to complete the FAFSA for each year you’re enrolled in school. You may need to meet certain eligibility requirements, such as income limits, to get some grants. The FAFSA is how you apply for the Pell Grant, which is a financial need-based grant. The FAFSA also determines eligibility for federal work-study, which is a job program rather than a grant.

Recent findings suggest that federal aid, including federal grants, typically requires students to meet satisfactory academic progress. This means you have to maintain a minimum grade point average and be on track to finish your degree on time, as determined by your school. Your school also sets how many credits you must take to qualify for grant funding.

Some grants — typically private or institutional grants — require an additional application that asks for transcripts, letters of recommendation and personal essays. Your school’s financial aid office or the grant provider will have details on applying for specific grants.

After you submit the FAFSA, you’ll receive a financial aid award letter from each school you applied to, which outlines how much in federal, state and institutional grants you’ve been offered. You must accept your aid to receive it.

Most grants will be disbursed directly to your college or university. Your school will apply the grant money first to tuition, fees and any other charges it bills, such as housing or a meal strategy.

Sources indicate that in some cases, you may receive more grant money than your school bills, which is the best-case scenario. If that happens to you, any leftover funds will likely be refunded to you. Refund timelines vary by school, so it may take some time to get your money. You can get your refund faster by setting up direct deposit with your school. You can then use the funds for other costs approved by your grant — some examples are detailed below.

If you have questions about your grant money, contact your college’s financial aid office.

Grants can help cover cost-of-attendance expenses. Generally, you can use grant money to pay for tuition, textbooks, class materials, transportation, housing and food. Depending on your school’s policies, you can use grant money to cover summer classes or study abroad programs, too.

Some grants come with specific terms about how you can spend them. Check your financial aid award letter or, for a private or institutional grant, the school’s or organization’s website to find specifics.

Expenses grants aren’t meant for:.

Recent findings suggest that after your grant is applied to your tuition and school expenses, you can options to fill the gaps between what the grant covers and the total cost of your program. Some options include savings, scholarships, work-study, payment intends, federal student loans or, as a last resort, private loans. By using grants to pay for your college education, you may be able to borrow less.

To maximize the grants you’re eligible to receive, enter accurate information on the FAFSA and complete it as soon as you can — some funds are first-come, first-served. Also, don’t limit yourself to federal or state grants — search and apply for as many privately funded grants as you can find.

According to recent reports, your grant money usually goes straight to your college or university to pay your tuition and fees. Anything that is left over may be disbursed to you for other school-related costs.

Yes, but it depends on your grant. Housing is part of your cost of attendance, so you can use grant money to pay for off-campus rent.

According to recent reports, you don’t have to pay back a grant as long as you continue to meet all requirements for the grant, such as staying enrolled. You can use grant money on school and school-related expenses. Some grants may require you to meet eligibility requirements such as a minimum GPA or state residency. If you receive more grant money than your cost of attendance for a given school term, ask your financial aid office if you can put that grant money toward next year’s cost of attendance.

If you have a federal grant like a Pell Grant, these are examples when you may have to repay all or part of the grant:.

You withdrew from your program.

You received enough scholarship money to reduce your federal aid need.

Sources indicate that it depends. You can usually use grant money to buy a laptop. Computers are considered course materials, which fall under cost-of-attendance expenses, so they can be covered by a grant. However, always double-check with the grant provider and your financial aid award letter to ensure that you’re following all restrictions. Whether you can use grant money to cover a laptop depends on your school’s policies and how much grant money you receive.

Industry observers note that if you get more grant money than your school bills you, you’ll likely receive the leftover money to spend on other cost-of-attendance expenses. You can use this money on living costs such as transportation or housing. Grant money often goes mostly toward tuition, so a refund isn’t guaranteed.

Grant and scholarship money is generally tax-free when you use it for tuition, required fees, books and required class supplies. If you have additional questions, consider talking to a tax professional.

By Thomas Niel – Nov 26, 2026 at 5:30AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Realty Income ›.

Besides its reputation as one of the best monthly dividend stocks, Realty Income (O +1.18%) often increases its dividend. In the recent past, the real estate investment trust (REIT) has raised its monthly payout quarterly.

Although these payout increases are relatively slight, they do provide a bit of a boost if one's objective is to build a steady income-generating machine out of a Realty Income position. For instance, just investing $200 per month in this REIT, starting now, could create an asset that generates $150 in monthly dividend income by 2036.

Sources indicate that currently, Realty Income pays a monthly dividend of $0.274 per share. Annualized, that's about $3.29 in cash dividends. With this REIT recently trading for about $60 per share, this works out to a forward annual dividend yield of about 5.5%.

NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

Let's say you invested $200 per month in Realty Income. Making several assumptions, such as 1% annualized share price appreciation, in line with historic performance, plus 3.5% average annual dividend growth, after 10 years you would own about 515 shares, worth roughly $30,900. With estimated monthly dividends of $0.30 per share by year 10, this position would generate an estimated $154.50 per month in dividend income.

It has been revealed that the good news about this strategy is the high likelihood that Realty Income's slow-and-steady growth trend will persist for yet another decade. Since going public in 1994, Realty Income has raised its monthly dividend 117 times. As it sticks to its strategy of geographic and property diversification, the REIT appears well-positioned to maintain its dividend growth streak.

In a recent development, the key downside of this plan is the opportunity cost. Realty Income may sport a high yield, but it has underperformed in terms of share price growth relative to the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.25%)index. Even if you are willing to trade potential returns for lower volatility, consider weighing it against other options, such as dollar-cost averaging into dividend-focused index funds.

Industry News: Mortgage Rates Today, Wednesday, November 25: A Little Lower

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mortgage rates are a little lower this morning, and where they'll go next isn't totally clear.
  • Industry observers note that the average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 7.05% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow.
  • Industry observers note that inflation data out this morning looks, at first glance, like bad news for mortgage rates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mortgage rates are a little lower this morning, and where they'll go next isn't totally clear.

Industry observers note that the average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 7.05% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is eight basis points lower than yesterday and 33 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.).

Industry observers note that inflation data out this morning looks, at first glance, like bad news for mortgage rates. But depending on how markets react, we could actually see lower mortgage rates. Keep reading after the charts for all the details.

Below are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for perspective.

P.S. Markets will be closed tomorrow for Thanksgiving, and Black Friday's a half day, and mortgage rates don't move much when the markets aren't moving. I won't be here to talk to you about mortgage rates, either, 'cause NerdWallet gives us Thursday and Friday off. Happy Thanksgiving!

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders.

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

According to recent reports, like I mentioned above, it's not totally obvious where mortgage rates will head next. Let's walk through the two scenarios.

Sources indicate that here's why rates could go up: This morning, we got October's Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, also known as PCE. It's the last measure of inflation to come out each month, but it's also the Federal Reserve's preferred metric, so PCE gets a lot of attention.

The stats came in mostly as predicted, though it's not like the predictions were good — inflation's been overly strong for a while. But the core year-over-year figure, which came in a tenth of a percent over predictions, could prove troublesome. Core PCE removes categories that can be extra volatile, so it's considered a measure that reveals the underlying trend. In this case, the underlying trend is Not Good.

According to recent reports, it's already pretty much a lock that we'll see a rate hike at the Federal Reserve's December meeting, because yes, raising the federal funds rate is the Fed's main tool for taming inflation. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but a rate-hiking cycle from the central bankers definitely keeps upward pressure on borrowing costs.

Sources indicate that on the other hand, here's why that same inflation data could help rates go down: Over the past several days, we've watched the stock market go on a wild ride, with the Anthropic IPO and the return of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Yesterday, things weren't looking good for tech stocks, and these inflation numbers could make it even worse.

The amount that tech companies have borrowed to fund AI buildout is a significant concern for investors, since companies will have to cover those costs before investors see any profits. It's already a big task, and if everything costs more thanks to inflation, it's that much harder.

This AI-related anxiety is rough on the stock market, but it's been a boon for Treasury bonds. More demand for bonds pushes up bond prices, which brings down bond yields (basically, the return investors get on a bond). Mortgage rates for 30-year loans are generally benchmarked to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, so here's why you care about all of this: Lower Treasury yields means lower mortgage rates, too. If investors keep stressing about inflation eating into tech profits, we could see mortgage rates continue to move lower.

That was a lot of info on inflation, but inflation's not the only major metric influencing rates.

Let's back up for a second. The Federal Reserve tries to keep the economy steady by focusing on two key goals, often referred to as the Fed's dual mandate. One side is price stability — keeping inflation reasonable. The other is maximum employment, meaning those who want to work are able to find jobs.

Next week we'll shift our focus to the employment side of the Federal Reserve's mandate, because the first week of the month is always all about employment data. On Tuesday, Dec. 1, we'll kick things off with the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS). JOLTS can tip us off to trends in the labor market; stuff like whether folks are leaving jobs voluntarily or if companies have openings that are going unfilled.

On Wednesday, payroll firm ADP will release its monthly employment stats. ADP is looking at its own payroll data to get an idea of how the job market is growing or contracting. The numbers don't include the public sector, but ADP often provides a preview of how the jobs report will go.

The Employment Situation Summary, better known as the jobs report, drops on Friday. This is the massive one, since it tells us the nation's unemployment rate. The jobs report's other major stat is, similar to ADP, how many jobs the economy added or lost in the previous month. Unlike ADP though, the jobs report is inclusive of everybody in the public and private sectors.

Sources indicate that lately the labor market's been looking super healthy, which is great news for the economy but less positive for mortgage rates. When hiring's strong, the Fed can feel safer raising the federal funds rate (that's the short-term borrowing rate the central bankers adjust). Higher rates tend to discourage businesses from borrowing and expanding, so if the job market's on shaky footing, the central bankers are going to be cautious about raising the benchmark rate.

What we're seeing now though, where inflation is clearly the problem and employment's just fine, is a recipe for higher rates. Again, the Fed doesn't control mortgage rates, but the central bank being in rate-hike mode puts upward pressure on mortgage rates.

In a recent development, if we were to see employment falter in this latest round of numbers, it still probably wouldn't change the Fed's initiative. That would be one poor month for the labor market versus months upon months of inflation running rampant — so yeah, they'll keep an eye on jobs, but inflation's still the scourge.

Our most likely source of lower mortgage rates in the short term is what I described above; investors who are leery of inflation and the promise of AI looking to the safe harbor of the bond market.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates.

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you could start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.55% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Industry observers note that also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

Industry observers note that » Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders.

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

According to recent reports, if the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a fresh home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

Recent findings suggest that » Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis.

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

Industry observers note that 🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

In addition to market factors outside of your control, your customized quote depends on your:.

    Industry News: If an AI Bubble Bursts, This Is the Only Tech Stock I Want to Own

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that if construction activity at every half-built AI data center in America went quiet, which tech giant would feel it least?
    • The mood on Wall Street has swung hard.
    • Sources indicate that to be clear: If the AI boom keeps roaring, there will be faster growers in substantial tech than Apple.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Micah Zimmerman – Nov 26, 2026 at 5:46AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Apple ›.

    Sources indicate that if construction activity at every half-built AI data center in America went quiet, which tech giant would feel it least? I've chewed on that question a lot as tech stock prices have whipsawed this fall, and my answer keeps coming back to one name: Apple (AAPL +0.43%).

    The mood on Wall Street has swung hard. A broad tech sell-off pushed all three major indexes into correction territory, and the leadership whirlwind at Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%), which ended with its board reinstating CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, showed how much of the market now hangs on one AI story. Apple, meanwhile, still trades within a few percentage points of its 52-week high.

    Sources indicate that to be clear: If the AI boom keeps roaring, there will be faster growers in substantial tech than Apple. This is about the one tech stock I'd want to hold if it doesn't.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    According to recent reports, the AI race has turned Apple's megacap peers into construction companies. Alphabet (GOOGL -2.13%) is on course to spend between $195 billion and $205 billion on capital expenditures this year, mostly on AI, and it posted negative free cash flow last quarter. So did Meta Platforms (META +3.40%).

    Apple spent about $9 billion on property and equipment in its entire fiscal 2026 — that’s less than it laid out the year before. Instead of building data centers and developing upcoming foundation AI models, the iPhone maker rents what it needs. It struck a deal to base its next foundation models on Google's Gemini after deciding "Google's AI technology provides the most capable foundation." That's the honest weak spot. Apple was late to the generative AI party, the debut of its upgraded Siri slipped by a full year, and it leaned on a rival to catch up.

    In a recent development, but being late can mean being cheaper. Much of Apple's AI runs on the device itself.

    Industry observers note that "On device -- it's very, very efficient. No real costs associated with that," CFO Kevan Parekh noted on the November earnings call. Businesses are noticing, too. Gap (GAP +2.52%) is running its AI loss-prevention models on Mac Minis across hundreds of stores, "eliminating cloud token costs," Parekh said. CEO John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September, put it simply: "Apple devices, we think, are the best places to use all forms of AI.".

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    Apple's real defense is the 2.5 billion active devices in people's pockets and on their desks.

    According to recent reports, "Thanks to our very high levels of customer satisfaction and loyalty, our installed base of active devices reached a new all-time high," Parekh stated. Those customers carry more than 1.5 billion paid subscriptions, and Apple’s services segment revenue hit a record last quarter with a 76% gross margin. Ternus calls the iPhone an "intelligent personal hub," noting that "so much of your personal data is on your iPhone.".

    Services isn't bulletproof, though. Parekh flagged headwinds from third-party licensing, softer mobile gaming, and an unfavorable U.S. court ruling on App Store payment links.

    Recent findings suggest that then there's the cash. Apple ended the quarter with $137 billion in cash and securities on its books against $80 billion in debt, and it returned $28 billion to shareholders, including $24 billion in stock buybacks. The organization’s approach, Parekh noted, is to "invest in our business and return excess cash to shareholders.".

    Here's the twist I find most interesting: The AI infrastructure build-out is hurting Apple right now because data centers are gobbling up so many memory chips.

    "What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented," Ternus noted, adding that "we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase." Apple expects lower gross margins this quarter, primarily due to memory costs, and has already raised prices on iPhones, Macs, and iPads to reflect its higher costs.

    Sources indicate that none of that makes the stock cheap. Trading at about 39 times earnings, Apple carries a premium P/E ratio, and during real market panics, pricey stocks get sold along with everything else. Apple stock could still fall if an AI bubble bursts. The case I’m making is that its business wouldn't.

    When I picture the AI party ending, I see builders writing down the value of their data centers and one company with 2.5 billion customers paying less for memory and renting AI from whichever infrastructure players survive. That's the side of the table I'd want to be sitting on.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When it’s cold outside, it’s the ideal time to stay home, organize your finances, set some latest money goals and make progress toward them.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When it’s cold outside, it’s the ideal time to stay home, organize your finances, set some latest money goals and make progress toward them.

    That’s the promise of the viral winter money trend known as “The Great Lock In” that’s circulating on social media.

    Recent findings suggest that “You’re probably not doing too much,” claims Robert Baird, wealth manager at Cornerstone Financial Services in Southfield, Michigan. “It gets dark early. So those can be great months to lock into saving and not spend in excess.”.

    One notable component of the Great Lock In is developing fresh routines that will last well into 2027, says Jordan Mangaliman, founder and fiduciary wealth advisor at GoldLine Wealth Management in Fullerton, California.

    “We want a long-term habit versus a Band-Aid fix,” he notes. “In today’s economy, money goes in and out so blindingly fast.”.

    Recent findings suggest that ready to join the movement? Here’s how to get started.

    According to recent reports, what’s your money moonshot? Maybe it’s paying off all your credit card debt or purchasing a home. Or spending less than you earn. Defining it is the first step toward achieving it.

    Recent findings suggest that “Spend a lot of time identifying what that goal is,” Baird says. “Everyone’s in a different position, so comparing yourself to what you see online might not be applicable.”.

    Even while setting ambitious money goals, it’s worth grounding them in reality, Mangaliman notes.

    If you want to save a larger portion of your income, he suggests trying the new saving pattern for a couple of months to see how it feels rather than saying you’ll do it forever and then getting frustrated.

    “It’s a marathon, not a sprint,” Mangaliman adds.

    Once you’ve outlined those big goals for your Great Lock In, create a budget to help you achieve them, Baird states.

    Sources indicate that he suggests combing through your previous credit or debit card spending to see where your money is going. Then you can decide what you want to change or shift. Using a tool like the 50/30/20 budget calculator can also help. This approach allots 50% of take-home pay toward needs, 30% toward wants and 20% toward savings and debt payments beyond the minimum.

    According to recent reports, baird suggests including saving as a line item in your budget so you don’t forget to do it. “Building that cost into your budget will put you in a better position later,” he says.

    Any Great Lock In should include growing your savings, because that makes achieving other goals easier, Baird states.

    Industry observers note that “Maybe there’s something you could cut in the short term to build up that savings,” he says. Good targets include subscription services, food delivery, entertainment and travel costs.

    Saving more is especially challenging in today’s environment, when everyday expenses like gas are higher than they were a year ago.

    Baird says that makes winter a good time to try to reduce costs. There can be fewer temptations to go out and spend money when the days are shorter and the temperatures are colder.

    Mangaliman recommends setting aside three to six months’ worth of expenses, although even a smaller amount is helpful. “Ultimately it’s about what you can afford,” he says. “It’s the foundation of your financial house.”.

    Along with building savings, paying down high-interest debt is another pillar of the Great Lock In.

    According to recent reports, with credit card interest rates higher than they were a few years ago, carrying credit card debt has gotten more expensive. “I would consider applying some savings to paying down debt, especially right now when your debt is costing you more than you can earn in savings,” Baird says. (You still want to reserve an emergency fund to cover unexpected expenses.).

    “High-interest debt is one of the biggest thieves of wealth,” Mangaliman indicates. And one way to avoid turning to debt again in the future is to build up that emergency fund so it’s there for you if you need it.

    Even when you are committed to a Great Lock In, some hiccups along the way are inevitable. Success depends on continuing anyway.

    “It’s like a diet,” Baird notes. “Just because you ate ice cream on a Sunday doesn’t mean on Monday you can’t go right back to being disciplined again.”.

    It has been revealed that “Be kind to yourself and do everything in moderation,” Mangaliman suggests. Just wanting to improve your finances is already a great first step, he states.

    In fact, he embraces the Great Lock In mentality himself. “There’s an old saying: It’s not how you start, but how you finish,” he notes. “And you want to finish the year on a strong note so you carry those habits into 2027 and beyond.”.

    #199828. Cathie Wood and Philippe Laffont Are on Opposite Sides of AMD Stock. Here's Who I Think Is Right.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (867 w)

    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fool ↗ Open Full Page

    Cathie Wood and Philippe Laffont Are on Opposite Sides of AMD Stock. Here's Who I Think Is Right.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 10 stocks we like better than Advanced Micro Devices ›.
    • Sources indicate that two substantial-name tech investors have landed in different places on Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -1.75%).
    • Recent findings suggest that the split follows a steep slide.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Daniel Sparks – Nov 26, 2026 at 5:53AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Advanced Micro Devices ›.

    Sources indicate that two substantial-name tech investors have landed in different places on Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -1.75%). Cathie Wood's Ark Invest added almost 50,000 shares of the chipmaker on Friday, Nov. 20, when the stock dropped 13%. Philippe Laffont's Coatue Management, though, owned no AMD shares at all at the end of September, according to its newest quarterly filing.

    Recent findings suggest that the split follows a steep slide. AMD's record close was on Oct. 6, at $649.42. As of this writing, the stock trades near $376, off about 42% over seven weeks.

    And in the third quarter, both investors sold. Only Wood has been reported buying back in since.

    It has been revealed that cathie Wood. Image source: Getty Images.

    Coatue's 13F filings (the quarterly forms major money managers use to disclose their U.S.-listed stock holdings) show a fund that has exited AMD twice in 2026. It ended 2025 with around 1.24 million AMD shares, a stake then worth $265 million, and it ended March with none.

    Industry observers note that that first exit looks badly timed now. The growth stock closed the first quarter at around $203 and almost tripled by the end of June. Even after this fall's sell-off, the stock trades well above its highest first-quarter close of about $260.

    It has been revealed that coatue did buy back in during that climb, ending June with about 96,000 shares worth about $56 million. But that was a small stake, roughly 0.1% of the $48.6 billion in holdings the filing highlighted.

    Sources indicate that and by Sept. 30, the position was gone again. AMD closed the third quarter at about $612, so the second exit has aged well, with shares off about 39% since.

    Sources indicate that A 13F shows holdings, not reasons. But Coatue's filing doesn't look like a pullback from chips. As of Sept. 30, the fund had over $3 billion each in Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, Micron Technology, and Lam Research. Laffont still seems to be betting significant on the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out. AMD just wasn't part of it when the quarter ended.

    In a recent development, ark has traded AMD in both directions this year. After buying shares in January and February, its funds sold AMD on dozens of days from late March to late October while the stock rose. The largest sale was on Sept. 29, around a week before the record close, when Ark sold 181,767 shares worth about $110 million.

    According to recent reports, then the buying began again. Ark picked up almost 49,000 shares on Nov. 5, a day AMD dropped 17%, and 49,745 more on Nov. 20.

    Sources indicate that valued at those days' closes, the two purchases came to about $41 million. Together, they equal a bit over half the shares Ark sold on Sept. 29 alone, bought back at closing prices 30% to 33% lower.

    AMD is now around 2% of the flagship ARK Innovation ETF, a far bigger part of the fund than the stake Coatue reported in June.

    The case for Wood's buy depends on how fast AMD's business is growing. Its data center segment, home to the company's Instinct AI chips and EPYC server processors, had record sales of $8.5 billion in the third quarter. Growth from the previous quarter has picked up all year, from around 7% in Q1 to 16% in Q2 and then 27% in Q3. Management expects about 50% sequential growth for the segment in the fourth quarter. And for 2027, it expects total revenue to climb over 80%, with data center making up more than 80% of sales.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    "It is true that demand is higher than supply," CEO Lisa Su stated during AMD's third-quarter earnings call.

    Demand that tops supply is promising, but it also means AMD's outlook relies on getting enough parts to make all those chips. Preparing for that growth is a drag on cash flow. Inventory climbed around $3 billion from the second quarter to $11.5 billion, and free cash flow dropped 64% year over year to $554 million.

    The price, meanwhile, has come down a long way. Measured against analysts' average 2027 estimate of around $17.60 per share, AMD's third-quarter close near $612 was almost 35 times earnings. The current price of $376 works out to about 21 times earnings on the same estimate.

    Ark's September sale and Laffont's second exit both look well timed so far. But for someone buying now, I think Wood is right. I'd consider buying AMD shares at this price, and I'd only rethink that if supply complications put its 2027 outlook out of reach.

    #199825. Latest Update: 4 Ways to Prep Your Finances Before the Next Tech Outage

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nerdwallet ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: 4 Ways to Prep Your Finances Before the Next Tech Outage

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (754 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.
    • Have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year?
    • It has been revealed that but what about your money?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.

    Have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year? Maybe.

    It has been revealed that but what about your money? If your area was hit by a natural disaster or your bank had an outage, are your finances ready?

    In a recent development, dan Stanush, senior financial planner at Charles Schwab in Asheville, North Carolina, recalls how fast financial conveniences disappeared after Hurricane Helene hit in 2024. “We lost power for three weeks and water for six weeks,” he said in an email. “And some local businesses could only accept cash or checks because card systems and ATMs were down.”.

    According to recent reports, don’t get caught unprepared. Here are the moves experts suggest to help you weather various types of emergencies:.

    It has been revealed that last week’s Chase outage was a good reminder that access to your bank balance can be disrupted. Stash at least enough cash at home — in small bills — to cover one week of expenses, notes Jeff Judge, a certified financial planner (CFP) with Chesapeake Financial Planners in Forest Hill, Maryland.

    In a recent development, if systems go down, ATMs can go down with them, stated Eileen Olson, a CFP with Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina, in an email. Keeping cash in a safe at home is a good blueprint, but it’s also smart to carry cash when you travel. (Remember when planes were grounded nationwide a week and a half ago?).

    According to recent reports, “My parents and sister were traveling overseas on 9/11 and got stuck much longer than they expected,” Olson said. “After that, they always traveled with more cash.”.

    If your primary bank and its app were down, would you be able to pay bills? Having an account at more than one bank gives you an alternate funding source. Consider opening a high-yield savings account at a second bank or credit union for your emergency fund.

    “This is the step I push hardest,” Judge states. “I had a client whose debit card, credit card and savings all ran through one bank, so when that bank’s system went down, she couldn’t even buy gas.”.

    If you don’t want to open a second bank account, a second credit card from a different bank and preferably on a different network (i.e. Visa vs. Mastercard) can provide another way to pay for things. “If there’s a problem with one credit card network, I have a backup with two other credit cards,” states Tony Steuer, author of “Get Ready! A Step-by-Step Planner for Maintaining Your Financial First Aid Kit.”.

    Make a printed list of your accounts, along with account numbers and key contact numbers. Include your bank, insurers, credit card companies and any financial professionals. Store the list with copies of essential paperwork, including insurance policies and their declarations pages, estate planning documents, legal certificates and identification — potentially in a fire-resistant file box.

    Sources indicate that keep a digital copy of your documents in a password-protected, encrypted spot as well. A password manager can store all of your login info.

    Joon Um, a CFP with Secure Tax & Accounting in Beverly Hills, California, suggests digital storage site Everplans to his clients, but there are a variety of sites that offer encrypted document storage.

    Industry observers note that take some time to write down how you’d pay for groceries, gas and medication if your usual payment methods weren’t available. What expenses would you need to cover first? What recurring bills are on autopay? Where would you keep the cash and any key documents you’d want to take with you if you had to leave home? Make sure other household members know where everything is.

    And set a reminder to enhancement your records at regular intervals. Steuer, for instance, saves his account statements as PDFs and prints everything out once a year. “One of the significant concerns is that people could conceivably break into your 401(k) and drain your 401(k) account,” he says. Account statements could help if a hack affects any financial balances.

    It all adds up to a web of protection that (hopefully) you’ll never have to use.

    “The goal is not to anticipate every scenario,” stated Schwab's Dan Stanush, “but to have enough flexibility to meet basic needs while systems come back online.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Anthropic (ANT +1.08%) just set a record for the largest amount of capital raised in an IPO.
    • In a recent development, like many IPO stocks, Anthropic enjoyed a first-day pop, sending the shares to $97.17 at the close.
    • In a recent development, but investing in mega-IPOs like Anthropic after their debut isn't always a great decision.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Adam Levy – Nov 26, 2026 at 6:04AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›.

    Anthropic (ANT +1.08%) just set a record for the largest amount of capital raised in an IPO. The AI lab's offering raised $81 billion, topping the $75 billion raised by Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.30%) earlier this year. Anthropic also took in about $26 billion in cash from a separate private placement with several big tech companies.

    In a recent development, like many IPO stocks, Anthropic enjoyed a first-day pop, sending the shares to $97.17 at the close. That could leave many investors with FOMO, as the AI lab looks to inject newly introduced life into AI stocks that have been sluggish over the last few weeks.

    In a recent development, but investing in mega-IPOs like Anthropic after their debut isn't always a great decision. Here's what history claims about buying into big IPOs.

    In a recent development, IPO stocks don't have a great track record. Investors often end up losing money on their investments after three years. Indeed, 60% of all IPOs between 1975 and 2021 ended with prices below their first-day close after three years of trading publicly.

    The odds are much better for bigger companies. Companies with at least $1 billion in sales (adjusted for inflation) saw an average three-year buy-and-hold return of 32.4% from their first-day closing price, well above the 17.8% average for IPOs with less than $1 billion in trailing-12-month sales. That said, the average mega-IPO still produces an average return below the rest of the market in its first three years of trading.

    Sources indicate that recent history hasn't been too kind either. SpaceX and SK Hynix (SKHY -0.75%) had two of the largest IPOs in history this year. As mentioned, SpaceX raised $75 billion when it went public in June. While SK Hynix traded on the Korean stock exchange, its Nasdaq debut raised an additional $26.5 billion by making it easier for American investors to buy the stock. Today, both stocks trade below their first-day closing price.

    According to recent reports, the table includes the 10 largest IPOs on U.S. stock exchanges of the last 15 years:.

    *Less than one year since IPO, returns are to date.Data source: Renaissance Capital and Google Finance.

    As you can see, the track record isn't great for the biggest U.S. IPOs, which tend to generate significant media attention and investor buzz. As such, the stocks are priced rather than valued, and with so much excitement about the companies, that excitement can push prices well above fair value.

    While history isn't kind to the biggest IPOs, investors need to evaluate stocks on a case-by-case basis. Anthropic's valuation was previously floated at around $2 trillion before AI stocks began facing selling pressure amid financing concerns and potential regulatory hurdles following the midterm elections. At a fully diluted market cap of around $1.8 trillion after its first day of trading, Anthropic hasn't been immune to those pressures.

    Sources indicate that but Anthropic is arguably well positioned to handle financing challenges. It now holds $232 billion in cash and equivalents on its balance sheet. What's more, it has financing in place using convertible note purchase agreements with multiple strategic partners totaling $77 billion.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    Industry observers note that that stated, Anthropic will have to continue growing revenue at an extremely rapid pace over the next five to 10 years while demonstrating considerable operating leverage. That's definitely possible based on its recent results, but there are significant risks in forecasting the future of a rapidly evolving industry. That means Anthropic shares are likely to be highly volatile in the near term, which may present a better buying opportunity than right after its IPO.

    #199816. Breaking: 3 Investing Moves All Investors Should Make Right Now if a Bear Market Is Coming

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (718 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fool ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: 3 Investing Moves All Investors Should Make Right Now if a Bear Market Is Coming

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, nobody can predict exactly when the next bear market will hit, but that doesn't mean investors should wait to prepare for it.
    • To that end, here are three investing moves to help protect portfolios today.
    • Cash is often put to use during bull markets because it doesn't offer the same excitement as fast-growing stocks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Rick Orford – Nov 26, 2026 at 6:19AM EST.

    In a recent development, nobody can predict exactly when the next bear market will hit, but that doesn't mean investors should wait to prepare for it. After all, if market volatility continues to rise, having the right strategy can make a major difference.

    To that end, here are three investing moves to help protect portfolios today.

    Cash is often put to use during bull markets because it doesn't offer the same excitement as fast-growing stocks. But when markets become volatile, having some extra cash on the side can be a huge advantage.

    For one, cash can help investors avoid selling long-term holdings if they need money during a downturn. But more importantly, it gives investors flexibility to buy quality companies at a discount and hold them over the long run.

    Sources indicate that plus, instead of trying to time the exact bottom, investors can invest gradually. This approach can help ease the pressure of making one huge investment decision at the wrong time.

    That said, investors should be careful about using leverage as a shortcut to protect their portfolios or profit from a potential market reversal. In fact, if the market moves against investors, these investments can rapidly see losses accelerate.

    Another way to manage risk is to spread it across different companies.

    Artificial intelligence (AI) has been a powerful driver of recent market rallies. However, these rallies have been concentrated in a few of the world's biggest companies. That alone creates potential risks.

    Specifically, if investor expectations around AI spending reset lower, valuations could take a bigger hit than the broad market might. Still, for investors, the takeaway isn't necessarily to abandon high-growth tech stocks. Instead, it's to avoid having an entire portfolio depend on a single name or theme.

    Recent findings suggest that investors might consider spreading their exposure across less correlated sectors such as healthcare, consumer staples, and financials. After all, these businesses have different economic drivers, which can help reduce the impact of weakness in any single industry.

    Additionally, it's worth looking beyond individual stocks. Broad-market exchange-traded funds (ETFs), for example, can provide exposure to companies across multiple industries, while bond funds and cash equivalents can add additional diversification. Doing so can help reduce portfolio volatility and limit the losses from any single investment.

    That brings us to another vital consideration: the quality of companies investors actually own.

    Sources indicate that when economic conditions worsen, companies with high debt, weak cash flow, and limited pricing power can find themselves under pressure. On the other hand, businesses with healthy balance sheets, strong competitive advantages, and recurring revenue may be better positioned.

    That's why investors should review a company's fundamentals before deciding whether to invest.

    Industry observers note that specifically, long-term investors should look for companies that generate consistent free cash flow (FCF), maintain manageable debt levels, and have business models that can survive economic downturns. For example, companies selling essential products and services are likely to be more resilient when households reduce their spending.

    That doesn't mean investors should automatically favor defensive stocks over growth companies. In fact, some long-term opportunities can still come from tech, industrials, and other high-growth industries. Ultimately, investors simply need to distinguish between companies benefiting from sustainable demand and those that rely mainly on hype.

    Of course, there's no guarantee that financially sound companies will avoid losses during a bear market, but focusing on the fundamentals gives investors a better starting point for finding companies worth holding through market volatility.

    Nobody knows for sure when the next bear market will come, but investors can already start preparing as early as today. In short, diversifying across sectors, prioritizing financially sound businesses, and maintaining cash reserves can help build a more resilient portfolio. Ultimately, the goal isn't to avoid every market decline, but to be in a stronger position when a bear market comes.

    #199813. Tech Report: Warren Buffett Told Savers to "Rejoice When Markets Decline." After the 2000-2002 Bear Market, the S&P 500 Doubled in 5 Years.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (631 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Fool ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Warren Buffett Told Savers to "Rejoice When Markets Decline." After the 2000-2002 Bear Market, the S&P 500 Doubled in 5 Years.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (631 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, at first blush the suggestion is counterintuitive.
    • As has been the case so often since taking the helm at Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.54%)(BRKB +0.37%) back in 1970, however, this bit of advice first dished out by Warren Buffett in his 1997 letter to Berkshire shareholders was eventually vindicated.
    • Granted, it was three years too early.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By James Brumley – Nov 26, 2026 at 6:29AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›.

    In a recent development, at first blush the suggestion is counterintuitive. A falling market is certainly nothing for investors to celebrate.

    As has been the case so often since taking the helm at Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.54%)(BRKB +0.37%) back in 1970, however, this bit of advice first dished out by Warren Buffett in his 1997 letter to Berkshire shareholders was eventually vindicated.

    Granted, it was three years too early. The tech-driven rally underway at the time carried on and even accelerated into the early 2000s. That's when it all unraveled. From that year's peak to 2002's trough, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.25%) fell on the order of 40%. Then five years following that multiyear low, the index had reclaimed everything it lost, rewarding those investors with enough forethought to celebrate the opportunity by diving into beaten-down stocks.

    It certainly wasn't the first time something like this had happened either.

    Recent findings suggest that the irony? By the time the S&P 500 had doubled its 2002 low by mid-2007, the next cyclical headwind -- led by the subprime mortgage meltdown -- was already underway. Less than two years later, the index had lost a little more than half of 2007's peak value. And once again it was destined for a major recovery. Only this time, the S&P 500 would only need four years to recover, and would ultimately go on to quadruple its 2009 low before the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic finally brought the rally to a screeching halt in early 2000.

    Even then, though, the pandemic-prompted bear market that pulled the S&P 500 down by one-third of its value would erase that loss before the end of the same year, en route to what would be a bull market worth 90% in less than two years. The 2022 bear market also dialed the index back by more than 20%, but the bull market since then is up more than 100% from the late-2022 bottom.

    The point is, every major and minor setback the stock market has suffered so far has eventually been recouped, and then surpassed.

    It's not like Buffett doesn't take his own advice either. He famously bought a stake in then-deeply-discounted Goldman Sachs back in 2008, and locked in a 60% gain on this position in 2020. Berkshire added a bunch of now-privately-held construction materials companies between 2000 and 2002 as well, positioning it for a couple of waves of housing booms that would materialize in the meantime.

    It has been revealed that the point is, while corrections and bear markets feel pretty miserable at the time they're happening, Warren Buffett is right -- they're a reason to rejoice, particularly if you missed out on most of the bull market that preceded them. Dips are a second chance to step in at a discounted price regardless of how major or small they are.

    Just don't get too cheeky or clever when this window of opportunity opens. No one knows exactly when or where a bottom is going to be made, and plenty of investors have missed out because they were holding out for slightly better prices that never materialized. Any decent dip that offers an entry price you can live with in the long run is more than good enough.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • During the first year of each of President Donald Trump's two nonconsecutive terms, he spearheaded the passage of a flagship tax and spending law.
    • According to recent reports, meanwhile, the "Massive, Beautiful Bill" (signed July 2025) made the personal income tax brackets from the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act permanent, as well as introduced a bevy of temporary tax breaks for calendar years 2025 through 2028.
    • President Trump's Big, Beautiful Bill has created some unsightly problems for Social Security.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Sean Williams – Nov 26, 2026 at 6:36AM EST.

    During the first year of each of President Donald Trump's two nonconsecutive terms, he spearheaded the passage of a flagship tax and spending law. The first, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (signed December 2017), permanently lowered the peak marginal corporate income tax rate from 35% to 21% and has been the catalyst behind record share buybacks on Wall Street.

    According to recent reports, meanwhile, the "Massive, Beautiful Bill" (signed July 2025) made the personal income tax brackets from the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act permanent, as well as introduced a bevy of temporary tax breaks for calendar years 2025 through 2028. While Trump's newest law is helping some taxpayers retain more of their income, it's also projected to drop a $169 billion bombshell on Social Security.

    President Trump's Big, Beautiful Bill has created some unsightly problems for Social Security. Image source: Official White House Photo by Joyce N. Boghosian.

    According to U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, more than 64 million tax returns for 2025 claimed at least one of the upcoming tax deductions or credits included in the Substantial, Beautiful Bill. The three best-known temporary breaks from 2025 through 2028 are:.

    While these tax breaks are helping tens of millions of Americans retain more of their income, they're hindering Social Security's primary income generator, the 12.4% payroll tax.

    Sources indicate that last year, the payroll tax accounted for over 91% of the $1.45 trillion in income collected. President Trump's Big, Beautiful Bill will narrow the pool of earned income subject to the payroll tax through 2028 -- and therein lies the problem.

    Sources indicate that shortly after the Massive, Beautiful Bill was signed into law by the president, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR) requested a financial outlook assessment on America's top retirement program by the Social Security Administration (SSA). In early August 2025, the SSA's Office of the Actuary (OACT) delivered a detailed 10-year projection.

    According to the SSA's OACT, Donald Trump's flagship law is estimated to increase costs for the program's trust funds by $168.6 billion from 2025 through 2034.

    US Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund Assets at End of Year data by YCharts.

    Furthermore, the OACT projected that the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance trust fund's asset reserve depletion timeline would shift forward, from the first quarter of 2033 to the fourth quarter of 2032, because of the Big, Beautiful Bill. The 2026 Social Security Board of Trustees Report confirmed this estimated shift in its June release.

    According to recent reports, to be clear, Social Security's litany of issues and its $29.3 trillion long-term funding shortfall primarily stem from several ongoing demographic shifts. This includes a decline in net migration into the U.S., historically low birth rates, and rising income inequality, among other factors. Trump's Massive, Beautiful Bill is a small piece of a very big problem.

    Nevertheless, Donald Trump's flagship tax and spending law has dug an even steeper hole for Social Security, and in six years (or potentially less), retirees may pay the price.
