    The latest 13F filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) are out, and a growing list of Wall Street financial institutions and billionaire hedge fund managers appear to be looking for ways to ramp up their exposure to Bitcoin (BTC +4.19%).

    One of the biggest names on that list is billionaire investor Paul Tudor Jones. From June 30 to Sept. 30, Tudor Investment doubled its stake in the iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT +0.92%). It now holds 1.36 million shares of the exchange-traded fund (ETF) valued at $64.6 million as of Sept. 30.

    So if billionaire hedge fund managers such as Paul Tudor Jones are buying Bitcoin, should you too?

    Bitcoin is right now trading 53% below its all-time high of $126,000. That's the bad news. The good news is that it has likely already bottomed at about $60,000.

    Sources indicate that tudor Investment was ramping up its exposure to Bitcoin at the same time the cryptocurrency was recording one of its best Augusts in recent memory. Bitcoin soared 25% during the month, eventually hitting $80,000.

    Recent findings suggest that but there's more to Bitcoin than just its upside potential. In the past, Jones has talked up the value of Bitcoin as a hedge against macroeconomic uncertainty and global instability.

    The billionaire hedge fund manager has even referred to Bitcoin as "unequivocally the best inflation hedge there is." And Jones has argued that Bitcoin should account for at least a tiny portion of any portfolio, given its unique hedging properties.

    It's notable to understand the broader context. First, the current Bitcoin ETF holdings of Jones (1.36 million shares) are nowhere near what they were in 2024. At that time, Tudor Investment held 8 million shares of the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF.

    Moreover, Bitcoin still accounts for just a tiny portion of the overall portfolio. According to the HedgeFollow database, Tudor Investment has total assets under management (AUM) of $23 billion. So its allocation to Bitcoin is well under 1% right now. Bitcoin doesn't even rank among the top 10 holdings.

    Although 13F filings can provide a broad overview of where a fund manager is putting money to work, they offer only a snapshot in time. In other words, a lot has happened since Sept. 30, and portfolio managers are constantly rebalancing their funds.

    As a result, we don't know if Jones moved out of Bitcoin before or after the midterm elections, or if he trimmed his Bitcoin position in response to the recent crypto sell-off.

    It has been revealed that still, the fact that Jones remains a supporter of Bitcoin is important. The world's most popular cryptocurrency has a unique combination of upside potential and downside protection and could be worth a closer look as a unique portfolio diversifier.

    #199797. The Biggest Mistakes Investors Make During a Market Crash, and How to Avoid Them.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (871 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Fool ↗ Open Full Page

    The Biggest Mistakes Investors Make During a Market Crash, and How to Avoid Them.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that when the stock market starts falling, investors face a difficult test.
    • Sources indicate that but market crashes also create opportunities.
    • Often, it comes down to three mistakes: trying to predict the bottom, selling because of fear, and buying cheap stocks without understanding why they are cheap.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Lawrence Nga – Nov 26, 2026 at 7:01AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Amazon ›.

    Sources indicate that when the stock market starts falling, investors face a difficult test. A 10% decline can promptly become 20%. Headlines grow increasingly negative, and even experienced investors begin to question their decisions.

    Sources indicate that but market crashes also create opportunities. Some excellent businesses become available at prices investors could only dream of during a bull market. So why do many investors fail to take advantage?

    Often, it comes down to three mistakes: trying to predict the bottom, selling because of fear, and buying cheap stocks without understanding why they are cheap.

    One of the biggest mistakes investors make is waiting for the perfect moment to buy. They want the market to fall further before investing. Then, when prices decline again, they become convinced that an even bigger crash is coming.

    Eventually, the market recovers, and they miss the opportunity altogether.

    Recent findings suggest that the problem is that nobody knows where the bottom is until it has already passed. Consider an investor who wants to buy shares in a organization trading at $100. The stock falls to $80, but the investor waits for $60. It then rebounds to $95.

    The investor was right that the stock had become cheaper, but waiting for the perfect price meant missing the opportunity.

    It has been revealed that A better approach is to focus on valuation rather than market timing. Decide what a business is worth and identify the price at which it offers an attractive potential return. If the shares reach that level, consider buying a portion of your intended position. If the price falls further and the investment case remains intact, you can consider adding more.

    This approach, often called buying in stages, removes the pressure to get the timing exactly right.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    Watching a portfolio lose value is uncomfortable. When a stock falls 30%, investors naturally wonder whether they should sell before things get worse. Unfortunately, fear can make a temporary decline feel like a permanent disaster.

    In a recent development, the vital question is not how much the share price has fallen. It is whether the business has deteriorated.

    According to recent reports, imagine owning shares in Amazon (AMZN -3.12%). During a recession, consumers may spend less, businesses may become more cautious, and technology stocks may fall sharply. But before selling, examine what is happening inside the company.

    Sources indicate that is AWS still attracting customers? Is Amazon maintaining its competitive position? Are consumers still buying things online? If the long-term investment case remains intact, a falling share price alone may not justify selling.

    According to recent reports, of course, this does not mean holding every stock through every downturn. Sometimes a falling share price reflects genuine problems: Customers are leaving, competitors are gaining ground, debt is becoming difficult to manage, or management has made poor decisions.

    So what to do? Whenever a stock you own falls sharply, revisit your original reasons for buying it. Compare the latest business performance with your expectations.

    It has been revealed that if the investment thesis is broken, consider selling. If the business remains healthy and the valuation is more attractive, holding or adding may make sense.

    In a recent development, A market crash can make almost everything look like a bargain. But some stocks fall for good reasons.

    According to recent reports, A firm might trade at just 5 times earnings, while its competitors trade at 20 times. At first glance, it looks cheap. However, what if its sales are declining, its debt is rising, and customers are moving to competitors?

    The low valuation may be justified because the business is losing its ability to generate profits. This is known as a value trap: A stock looks inexpensive, but its underlying business continues to deteriorate.

    Before buying a beaten-down stock, investors should examine at least four things:.

    Industry observers note that in short, don't buy a stock just because it has fallen 50%. Understand why it fell, examine its financial health, and decide whether the problem is temporary or structural.

    In a recent development, nobody knows exactly when the next market crash will happen, how far prices will fall, or when the recovery will begin. Trying to predict all three is an unnecessary burden.

    Instead, investors should focus on what they can control: understanding the businesses they own, knowing their value, and maintaining sufficient financial flexibility to capitalize on opportunities.

    A market crash can be frightening, but it does not have to be destructive. The biggest winners are not necessarily investors who buy at the absolute bottom. They are often those who avoid panic, recognize genuine bargains, and have the patience to let good businesses compound over time.

    Breakfast News: Talking Stocks Over Turkey

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1570 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By TMF Breakfast News – Nov 26, 2026 at 7:30AM EST.
    • Industry observers note that money talk often finds its way to the Thanksgiving table.
    • You don’t need a crystal ball to hold your own — just honest perspective from investors.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By TMF Breakfast News – Nov 26, 2026 at 7:30AM EST.

    Industry observers note that money talk often finds its way to the Thanksgiving table. One cousin wants stock picks, an uncle is calling a crash, and someone who’s never invested wants to know where to start.

    You don’t need a crystal ball to hold your own — just honest perspective from investors. So we asked our analysts how they’d build a portfolio from scratch, what drives their investing, and when a stock gave them the ick. Bring their answers to the table.

    It has been revealed that this one’s for the relative who just opened a brokerage account. Here’s how three analysts would start from scratch.

    Industry observers note that if I were starting from scratch as an investor now, I would build a three-stock portfolio that offers stability, diversification, and growth. Here’s what I would go for:.

    As one of the more value-oriented investors on the Hidden Gems team, I have quite a few stocks in my portfolio that could be considered to be excellent “beginner” stocks. But if I had to choose just three to start a portfolio with, they would likely be Berkshire Hathaway (BRKB +0.37%), Brookfield (BN +2.13%), and Realty Income (O +1.18%).

    Sources indicate that in reverse order, I would choose Realty Income because it’s an excellent compounder with a 30-year track record of excellent total returns, and Brookfield because it’s a great combination of reliable fee-based income and investments in some of the most promising types of real assets. Finally, Berkshire is like a well-diversified portfolio all in one stock, and I’ve said many times that if I could only own a single publicly traded company, it would be the one.

    According to recent reports, each quarter, the Stock Advisor team builds our list of Foundational stocks: 10 stocks that can form the basis of a well-diversified Foolish portfolio. That exercise is essentially the same as deciding what to buy when starting from scratch. It should be no surprise then, that my answer is obvious: Amazon (AMZN -3.12%) and Vertex Pharmaceuticals (VRTX +0.04%).

    Recent findings suggest that both of these businesses bring scale, leadership, and a credible path to decades-long success. They balance sector exposure and business-model risk while still putting capital toward companies with clear competitive advantages that are representative of some of the best the stock market has to offer. Two stocks do not a portfolio make, but I believe this is a strong starting point for many investors.

    Industry observers note that we asked our analysts what’s driving their investing this year. Their answers are worth borrowing as you strategy for 2027.

    Sources indicate that I will soon turn 54, and while I still feel like a kid, the fact is I’m not getting any younger. While I still love finding and investing in those great growth stories, I’m also slowly moving into more of a “protect your wealth” mindset.

    In a recent development, retirement isn’t even a word in my lexicon today; I love what I do and where I get to do it and will keep on doing it as long as the Fool will have me. But last year I set out to really focus on dividend exposure in my portfolio and 2027 is going to be another year where that remains a top priority. Rest assured I’ll be checking in on our Dividend Investor service quite frequently.

    I recently read a book called Sport’s Perfect Storm: An Industry Now Totally Adrift, by Roger Mitchell.

    This line caught my attention: “In everything, the past is always prologue.”.

    It has been revealed that after several years dedicated almost exclusively to reading investment books, this year, I’ve concentrated my leisure reading primarily on business history, and simply history. Learning about the past will give me a better perspective when investing for the future. Plus, this new focus feels particularly timely given that this year marks the 250th anniversary of American independence.

    According to recent reports, as the late Charlie Munger once mentioned: “There is no better teacher than history in determining the future. There are answers worth billions of dollars in a $30 history book.

    It has been revealed that I want to think through and take bigger, bolder investment decisions that will play out decades from now. I want to find the compounding decade busters! By doing the research and building the conviction, you can build the investment positions.

    However, then it takes discipline and patience to see those investments play out over the next few decades. It’s often so counterintuitive: you get super excited about something fresh (the dopamine hit) and then you have to wait … and wait … and wait (the sugar crash). Rome wasn’t built in a day, and neither was a truly Rule Breaking portfolio.

    According to recent reports, I turned 57 this year, which puts me within a decade of retirement. I also know that many workers are forced to retire sooner than expected. So it’s probably time for me to start reducing my risk by beginning to build a bond tent that will get me through the “retirement danger zone”: a time when a bear market could delay my plans or force me to sell investments when they’re down.

    However, like many Motley Fool members, I much prefer investing in stocks, and see investing in cash and bonds as the equivalent of being forced to eat broccoli because it’s good for me. (I don’t like broccoli.) So I will spend this year finding the balance between being prudent and pushing the envelope.

    Someone will ask if you’ve ever gotten one wrong. Here, three analysts share the moment a stock gave them pause, and what they did next.

    Alphabet (GOOG -2.02%) is one of my oldest, high-conviction portfolio positions. However, there was a period where I (along with many other investors) was concerned that its core search infrastructure might be unprepared for an AI universe disrupted by ChatGPT, despite it having invented much of the transformer architecture behind modern AI.

    Today, Alphabet is positioning Google Cloud as a primary growth engine, with an impressive backlog largely driven by enterprise AI adoption, it’s designing its own AI silicon through its custom TPUs, and is successfully integrating AI tools that keep owners within the Google ecosystem. While capex is substantial, it has the margins and cash position to maintain its trajectory without compromising a profitable growth story, and that’s a value proposition I continue to believe in.

    I first researched Pinterest (PINS +6.54%) in 2019 and was instantly enamored with the potential. The user base was smaller than other platforms, yet growing fast. And it was undermonetized. I called it an “exponential growth opportunity” because it could stack user growth on top of monetization growth.

    According to recent reports, my investment thesis for Pinterest appears broken, which is why I finally sold last year. Plenty of smart Fools think I’m wrong, and that may ultimately prove to be the case. But its most recent quarter revealed only 17% growth in ad impressions and a 4% drop in pricing. In my view, the platform is getting oversaturated with ads, and many advertisers still aren’t willing to pay a premium price after all these years.

    I’ve long admired Oracle’s (ORCL -5.13%) specialized “RDMA” server technology that’s so well suited to handle AI workloads, and in the several quarters since I finally bought in, my shares have appreciated handsomely. It’s loaded with debt however, and I’ve looked to super extended debt maturities as a mitigating factor. However, a slate of 2025 and 2026 borrowings for data center build-outs bent my buy thesis — I felt the “ick” after some back-of-the-napkin math!

    My thesis didn’t break, due to explicit capital allocation and free cash flow assurances the organization shared at its 2026 Investor Day in late October. But I continue to train a critical eye on capital expenditures, free cash flow, and the balance sheet strength of the cloud-based tech titans I own.

    It has been revealed that none of the analysts claim to know where the market is headed next — and that’s the point. They focus on businesses, not stocks, and make investment decisions accordingly.

    According to recent reports, you can bring that exact discipline and mindset to Thanksgiving. If someone asks what the market will do in 2027, it’s fine to skip the guesswork. Shift the question instead and ask, which businesses they’d want to own for the next decade, and why.

    That’s a conversation worth having over dessert. And for anyone just getting started, remind them that every great portfolio starts with a single first step.

    Sources indicate that from all of us at The Motley Fool, Happy Thanksgiving. Fool on!

    By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 26, 2026 at 7:34AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

    It has been revealed that jensen Huang's saga just took another unexpected turn. Nvidia's (NVDA -3.91%) board unanimously voted to reinstate him as CEO, less than a week after explicitly saying it wouldn't. The message the board is sending is clear. Despite Huang's extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy and with one of his subordinates, he is extremely valuable to the company. Just how valuable? The market's reaction to Huang's reinstatement gives us a clue.

    In a recent development, jensen Huang. Image source: Getty Images.

    It's no secret that Wall Street loves founder-led businesses, but why is that? There are several reasons. Let's discuss two of them. First, founders, who often own a substantial portion of the manufacturer, have a strong incentive to maximize shareholder value. Hired CEOs do too, to some extent. That's why equity-based compensation exists.

    However, founders tend to have more skin in the game. They wouldn't just lose their job if their corporation failed, unlike many hired CEOs. They would lose a substantial portion of their wealth. Second, founders often have a much deeper knowledge of the business they created, its characteristics, risks, competitive advantages, etc. That may give them an edge in leading the business to greater heights. According to some research, founder-led companies generally outperform broader equities.

    Industry observers note that so, Wall Street's faith isn't blind -- it is backed by data. That brings us back to Huang. He helped found Nvidia in 1993 and made it one of the most valuable companies in the world, and the corporation at the center of the ongoing artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. Huang is one of the longest-serving founder-CEOs in corporate America. That counts for a lot.

    Recent findings suggest that that's why the stock soared about 31%, gaining nearly $1 trillion in a single session, after it was declared that he was coming back. It was the largest single-day market-cap gain in history.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    Huang's return reduces the uncertainty tied to Nvidia's CEO search. Before the announcement, the market didn't know whether it would take six weeks or six months, and it was hard to reliably assign probability estimates to each outcome. The market abhors uncertainty, so the news had a major calming effect for many investors. That doesn't mean that Nvidia is out of trouble.

    According to recent reports, the company still faces major investigations tied to Huang's scandals, and the man is scheduled to testify before Congress soon. Still, with Huang at the helm -- and even accounting for ongoing regulatory probes -- the stock looks attractive. The first sign of that is Nvidia's financial results. In the third quarter of its fiscal year 2027, which ended on Oct. 25, Nvidia crushed expectations.

    The company's revenue soared 103% year over year to $115.8 billion, with data center revenue rising 110% compared to the year-ago period. Nvidia's non-GAAP gross margin remains exceptional for a company of this size at 74.9%, versus 73.5% in the year-ago period. Nvidia's non-GAAP earnings per share jumped 111% year over year to $2.68.

    Sources indicate that the company's AI tailwind is not slowing down much, if at all. It expects $130 billion in revenue for its fiscal year 2027 fourth quarter at the midpoint, representing a year-over-year increase of about 91%. Sure, that's a lower year-over-year revenue growth rate than in its recent third quarter, and so is Nvidia's 2028 fiscal year guidance of 75% year-over-year revenue growth.

    Industry observers note that but investors should remember two things. First, Nvidia tends to post stronger-than-expected results. It has done so more often than not for the better part of three years. So, a predicted 91% year-over-year growth rate may turn into something above 100% -- in fact, the manufacturer's Q3 2027 guidance implied its revenue would increase by about 89.5% compared to the year-ago period.

    Industry observers note that further, a decelerating growth rate may indicate tougher year-over-year comparisons rather than slowing demand for the company's products. Nvidia clearly still has a large market to tap into, and with Huang back at the helm, it is as well-positioned as ever to do so. And even after its 31% jump, the stock is down about 36% from the all-time high reached a little over a month ago. At current levels, Nvidia stock remains a buy.

    • It has been revealed that although Coca-Cola is up over 40% this year (as of Nov.
    • According to recent reports, you can count on one hand the number of brands more well-known globally than Coca-Cola.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Stefon Walters – Nov 26, 2026 at 7:39AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Coca-Cola ›.

    It has been revealed that I consider myself adventurous, but I often prefer boring when it comes to the stocks I own. I have my fair share of growth stocks, for sure, but my staple "boring" stock is Coca-Cola (KO -0.03%).

    It has been revealed that although Coca-Cola is up over 40% this year (as of Nov. 24), its main appeal has long been its dividend. It has increased its annual dividend for 64 consecutive years, making it one of the market's premier Dividend Kings ( companies with at least 50 consecutive years of dividend hikes). Considering that and its sustained success, it's a stock I'll never sell.

    According to recent reports, you can count on one hand the number of brands more well-known globally than Coca-Cola. Its products (especially its namesake soda) are available in virtually every part of the world, and its asset-light business model enables it to operate efficiently.

    Usually, if a tech giant wants distribution somewhere, it needs plants, warehouses, and delivery fleets in that market. In Coca-Cola's case, it relies on bottling and distribution partners to do so. Instead of owning factories and delivery fleets around the world, Coca-Cola sells concentrates and syrups to its partners and lets them do the heavy lifting.

    Keeping its business asset-light lets Coca-Cola maintain high margins and an ultra-safe dividend. You don't get to 64 years of dividend increases without consistent, high-margin cash flows.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    Not many companies fit the "recession-proof" narrative, but Coca-Cola is one of them. Even when the economy slows and money is tight, people still buy their favorite Coca-Cola brands. That's the beauty of its brand moat.

    Sources indicate that and despite being the undisputed leader in its space, Coca-Cola hasn't gotten complacent with its drink portfolio. It constantly refines its lineup to adjust to changing consumer preferences. Just six years ago, it had over 400 brands in its portfolio. Today, it has around half of that.

    When you have an option for virtually every occasion, you keep customers in your ecosystem. It's how the tech giant has sustained success for so long.

    According to recent reports, coca-Cola is a premium business that's priced like one. At the time of this writing, it's trading at 28.9 times its earnings, which is higher than its average over the past few years and higher than the S&P 500's (^GSPC -0.25%)23.7 P/E ratio. The stock is still a buy, but after a 40% run-up this year, the upside may be more limited. Luckily, that doesn't affect its dividend.

    Coca-Cola is always a good long-term investment, but with bear-market fears lingering, a short-term silver lining is that the stock typically outperforms the market during sell-offs. Past results don't guarantee future performance, but Coca-Cola has strong momentum at a time when the tech sector is dragging down the broader market.

    Is Anthropic Joining the S&P 500? Here's What Investors Need to Know.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Anthropic (ANT +1.08%) just completed the largest IPO in history, raising around $93.5 billion at $83 per share.
    • Given that it's now one of the largest publicly traded companies in the world, you might assume its addition to the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.25%) is imminent.
    • Industry observers note that when Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.30%) debuted earlier this year, there was a lot of discussion around how the major indexes would handle it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By David Dierking – Nov 26, 2026 at 8:03AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›.

    Anthropic (ANT +1.08%) just completed the largest IPO in history, raising around $93.5 billion at $83 per share. The stock closed Nov. 20 at $88.91.

    Given that it's now one of the largest publicly traded companies in the world, you might assume its addition to the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.25%) is imminent. It isn't, actually, and won't be for a while. But the stock will show up in several other major indexes within days.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    Industry observers note that when Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.30%) debuted earlier this year, there was a lot of discussion around how the major indexes would handle it. Typically, companies go public at much smaller market caps, not with market caps over $1 trillion. Index committees needed to decide whether to "fast track" these mega IPOs into the indexes sooner, given their outsize influence.

    Several providers made changes. But Standard & Poor's did not. It elected to keep the existing 12-month waiting period and generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) income requirements -- companies need to be profitable in the most recent quarter as well as the sum of the past four quarters in order to qualify.

    Anthropic, so far, falls far short on the GAAP income requirement, reporting a net loss of roughly $104 billion in the first nine months of this year.

    Given these requirements, the earliest we're likely to see Anthropic in the S&P 500 is late 2027.

    The S&P 500 will actually be the exception, not the rule, when it comes to adding Anthropic.

    The Nasdaq-100 index updated its inclusion criteria as a result of the SpaceX IPO. Now, if a manufacturer's entire market capitalization ranks within the top 40 current constituents in the index, it can be added to the index after just 15 trading days. Since Anthropic is listed on the Nasdaq, it could show up in the Invesco QQQ ETF (QQQ -0.65%) before the end of the year.

    Sources indicate that the Morningstar indexes, which acquired the widely-used CRSP indexes, could add Anthropic after the close of the fifth trading day. The Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF (VTI -0.18%) would be one of the biggest funds impacted by this. FTSE Russell works on a similar timeline.

    A lot of index funds will weight stocks according to the number of publicly available shares, not necessarily the total market cap. Since only about 5% of Anthropic's total market cap is now traded publicly, its starting weight will likely be small. Vanguard has projected only a 0.055% to 0.15% weighting for Anthropic in the Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF.

    When and if additional shares become publicly available, the anticipated weighting of these stocks would likely grow along with it.

    If you really want to own Anthropic, you should probably just buy Anthropic.

    The stock won't show up at all in the S&P 500 for the foreseeable future. For many of the major large-cap indexes and corresponding ETFs, the initial weight probably won't get much above 0.25%. The exception might be the Nasdaq-100, the Invesco QQQ ETF, and the Invesco Nasdaq 100 ETF (QQQM -0.66%). They could see an allocation closer to 1% given the more concentrated nature of that index.

    It'll likely be a similar story to what we saw when SpaceX went public: a lot of hype but minimal impact to the ETF marketplace and your portfolio in general.

    Long-term investors almost certainly shouldn't be making big asset allocation changes based on this. Even if you want to overweight tech based on a belief that Anthropic might spark the sector, your tech ETFs aren't going to meaningfully change in the future.

    #199772. Tech Report: Is Micron Stock a Buy After HPE Mentioned Memory Will Stay Scarce Into 2028?

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (856 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fool ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Is Micron Stock a Buy After HPE Mentioned Memory Will Stay Scarce Into 2028?

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (856 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE +1.57%) told investors on Nov.
    • "We expect supply of memory, NAND, and many other critical components to remain constrained to at least the second half of calendar 2028," CEO Antonio Neri noted on the organization's earnings call that evening.
    • That seems like good news for Micron Technology (MU -4.53%), which makes DRAM (the memory computers use while they work) and NAND flash storage chips.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Daniel Sparks – Nov 26, 2026 at 8:17AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Micron Technology ›.

    Industry observers note that hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE +1.57%) told investors on Nov. 23 that it still can't get all the memory chips it wants. And it doesn't think that'll change soon.

    "We expect supply of memory, NAND, and many other critical components to remain constrained to at least the second half of calendar 2028," CEO Antonio Neri noted on the organization's earnings call that evening.

    That seems like good news for Micron Technology (MU -4.53%), which makes DRAM (the memory computers use while they work) and NAND flash storage chips. But the memory maker's shares slid anyway. Micron closed at $707.70 on Nov. 23, just before the call. As of this writing on Nov. 25, the stock traded near $550, less than half the $1,213.56 it closed at on June 25, its record.

    Meanwhile, BNP Paribas downgraded the shares, saying memory supply might catch up to demand a year sooner than it had thought.

    In a recent development, the tech firm remarked in March that DRAM and NAND make up over half the cost of the parts in a traditional server. And its inventory more than doubled in fiscal 2026, from around $6.4 billion on Oct. 31, 2025, to $11.8 billion by July 31 and $14.1 billion by Oct. 31, 2026.

    Sources indicate that HPE's timeline seems to have stretched, too. In March, Neri stated he expected high DRAM and NAND prices to "persist well into 2027.".

    CFO Marie Myers mentioned the $14.1 billion inventory reflected higher costs for commodity parts like memory, purchases for customer orders, and what she called "strategic buys." She added that HPE's commodity costs climbed by significant double-digit percentages in 2026, and she expects smaller increases ahead. But smaller increases are still increases, not the price drops a glut would cause.

    According to recent reports, BNP Paribas thinks one could. In a note reported on Nov. 24, it cut its rating on Micron to neutral from outperform. It now states DRAM and NAND supply and demand might approach balance starting in mid-2027 and drive average selling prices down. It flagged risks to substantial cloud companies' data center intends for 2028 and newly introduced factory capacity coming online.

    Micron's stock dropped 11% that day, and again on Nov. 25, when research firm TrendForce said NAND flash might move into oversupply in 2027. TrendForce still expects DRAM to stay tight through 2027, and DRAM made up about three-quarters of Micron's revenue in fiscal 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that part of the new factory capacity BNP mentioned is Micron's own. Its first new fab in Idaho should start making wafers in mid-2027, and a facility in Taiwan should begin meaningful shipments around then too. But Micron says output at a new fab ramps up over a few quarters. And its other planned fabs, including a second one in Idaho and a new NAND factory in Singapore, aren't set to start output until the second half of 2028 or later.

    It has been revealed that "[W]e do not have line of sight to when supply and demand will return to balance," management wrote about DRAM in Micron's prepared remarks for its Sept. 30 earnings call.

    HPE's 2028 date matches Micron's building schedule. BNP's earlier date seems to rely more on demand weakening.

    Recent findings suggest that micron's fiscal 2028 ends on Aug. 31, 2028, so HPE's outlook covers nearly all of the year. If the outlook holds, Micron could spend most of fiscal 2028 selling into a market still short on chips. If BNP is right, prices could be dropping for most of it.

    The stock price looks closer to the second case.

    At roughly $550, Micron trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of about 7.4 on its fiscal 2026 results. Based on the average analyst estimate for fiscal 2028, the price is below 3 times earnings.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    Even BNP sees Micron's earnings per share bottoming at $86 in 2029, over the $74.33 per share Micron earned in fiscal 2026 under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP). The stock looks cheap even on that bearish estimate.

    One buyer's view could be wrong, of course. But I think HPE's outlook undercuts the glut worries, especially for DRAM, Micron's largest business. A buyer still stocking up at higher prices is tough to square with a stock priced for falling memory prices by mid-2027.

    I'd consider buying some Micron shares here, in a position small enough to ride out more days like Nov. 24. If HPE starts pulling that 2028 date forward, like BNP just did with its own, I'd rethink that.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (713 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fool ↗ Open Full Page

    Forget the Market's Hottest Stocks. This Boring Dividend Stock Is Where I'd Put $1,000 Before 2027.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (713 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 26, 2026 at 8:32AM EST.
    • It has been revealed that stock market volatility has ticked up dramatically in recent weeks, with the hottest stocks suddenly becoming some of the most volatile.
    • In a recent development, there are good reasons for Wall Street to be downbeat about PepsiCo.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 26, 2026 at 8:32AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than PepsiCo ›.

    It has been revealed that stock market volatility has ticked up dramatically in recent weeks, with the hottest stocks suddenly becoming some of the most volatile. If you are a long-term investor with a dividend focus and $1,000 to invest, you're better off taking a look at deeply unloved PepsiCo (PEP +0.88%). That will get you about seven shares.

    In a recent development, there are good reasons for Wall Street to be downbeat about PepsiCo. However, the company's long and successful history suggests that investors who think in decades, not days, will be well rewarded. Here's why you should buy it before the start of 2027.

    To get the bad news out of the way right up front, PepsiCo's business isn't doing particularly well right now. It isn't falling apart, either, but inflation, increasingly budget-conscious consumers, and shifts in consumer buying habits have taken a toll. In the third quarter of 2026, organic revenue growth was 3.1%. Coca-Cola (KO -0.03%), the tech giant's primary competitor in the beverage space, saw organic sales rise more than twice as fast, at 7%, in the same quarter.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    Simply put, investors are focusing on the industry leader and taking a show-me attitude with PepsiCo. You can see that in their valuations. For example, PepsiCo's dividend yield is 4.2% compared to Coca-Cola's 2.2%. Looking at more traditional valuation metrics, PepsiCo's price-to-sales ratio is just under 2x compared to a five-year average of 2.5x. Its price-to-earnings ratio is nearly 18x versus a five-year average of 25x. Coca-Cola's P/S ratio is 8x compared to a five-year average of 6.4x, and its P/E ratio is 28x compared to a five-year average of 26x. PepsiCo is cheap compared to its own history and relative to Coca-Cola.

    Sources indicate that that said, there are many reasons to like PepsiCo beyond valuation. For starters, as noted above, it isn't performing as well as Coca-Cola, but the firm isn't doing poorly. It is probably best to view it as muddling through a difficult period. It has done that many times before over the last 54 years. If that seems oddly specific, it is. That's the number of years this Dividend King has increased its dividend. Sure, that's a decade less than Coca-Cola, but it is hard to complain about PepsiCo's streak.

    Moreover, PepsiCo can stand toe-to-toe with Coca-Cola as a business. They are both industry leaders in brand strength, marketing prowess, innovation capabilities, and distribution. You aren't exactly stepping down to own PepsiCo. Meanwhile, PepsiCo offers you diversification that Coca-Cola does not. Coca-Cola is a beverage giant, but PepsiCo is a beverage giant (Pepsi), a snacking giant (Frito-Lay), and operates a large, well-respected packaged food business (Quaker Oats). For investors who value diversification, that may actually give it a leg up on Coca-Cola.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, it isn't like PepsiCo is sitting still and hoping conditions improve. It is actively working to shift its business in line with changes in consumer preferences. For example, it has acquired on-trend brands (Siete and Poppi), and it has been bringing out updated versions of existing brands, with a focus on healthier fare and protein. These are exactly the types of things that you would expect the manufacturer to do, but such moves can take time to play out.

    If you are looking to buy a stock and see it go up the next day, PepsiCo won't be a good option for you. The turnaround could take a year or more. However, you'll be collecting an attractive 4.2% dividend yield backed by a Dividend King with an industry-leading business while you wait. For patient dividend investors, this could be a very compelling long-term opportunity.

    It's been a wild couple of weeks for Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%), its shareholders, and Wall Street as a whole, to put it mildly.

    Following the admission of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, as well as allegations of two extramarital affairs with employees, Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12, spurring an elevator-down move in his organization's stock the likes of which have never been witnessed. Over 45 calendar days (ending Nov. 20), Nvidia lost $2.75 trillion in market value.

    Jensen Huang and Nvidia's board still have a significant problem on their hands. Image source: Official White House Photo by Joyce N. Boghosian.

    According to recent reports, then came the 180 on Monday, Nov. 23, with Nvidia's board reversing course and reinstating Huang as CEO after just 11 days. President Donald Trump congratulated the board on "what I consider to be an absolutely great decision," with a White House spokesperson claiming the president was involved in Huang's reinstatement as CEO.

    While Huang's return does resolve some near-term concerns for Nvidia, a critical problem remains that won't be easy to tackle.

    Nvidia didn't add more than $900 billion in market cap on Monday by accident. Huang has become the face of the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out, and his presence keeps Nvidia at the center of this multitrillion-dollar revolution.

    It has been revealed that “The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO… Congratulations to Jensen, the NVIDIA Board, to the People of the United States — and, indeed, the World!” - President DONALD J. TRUMP pic.twitter.com/bKAxuMr9aA.

    It has been revealed that jensen Huang leading the charge also means that Nvidia's aggressive innovation timeline stays on track. The company intends to bring an advanced AI chip to market annually, securing its top spot in graphics processing unit (GPU) compute capabilities.

    Recent findings suggest that perhaps most importantly, questions about the numerous circular financing deals Huang orchestrated are likely to die down. Nvidia has pledged jaw-dropping amounts of capital to neoclouds, hyperscalers, and large language model developers who, in turn, will purchase GPUs from the company.

    Huang's return, coupled with Nvidia's eye-popping growth forecast, suggests its stock is a bargain -- but that's not the full story.

    In a recent development, jensen Huang's biggest challenge awaits. Image source: Getty Images.

    Although Wall Street cheered this reinstatement, Nvidia committed the ultimate investing no-no: it broke investors' trust.

    Among billionaire Warren Buffett's laundry list of investing quotes, he once stated that "It takes 20 years to build a reputation and five minutes to ruin it." This month, we've had Nvidia's CEO and co-founder admit to an extramarital affair, have seen several probes kicked off by regulators into Nvidia's accounting and operating practices, and watched the company's board flip-flop on the company's longtime boss over a two-week stretch.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    What investor trust had been engendered has arguably been lost or damaged, and there's no quick fix for rebuilding it.

    Industry observers note that this intangible damage over the last couple of weeks may slow future circular financing deals, even with Jensen Huang back at the helm, and could further contract Nvidia's already historically low earnings multiple. Until Nvidia rebuilds trust with Wall Street and investors -- and there's no set timeline for this -- the upside for its stock and its dealmaking capacity may be capped.

    Investing $500 a Month in Coca-Cola, Realty Income, and Altria Could Generate Over $1,000 in Monthly Dividend Income by 2046

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that will you need dividend income at some point in the future?
    • That isn't necessarily the only way to meet your future income needs, though.
    • And while nobody can perfectly predict the future, your most promising dividend prospects for this purpose are Coca-Cola (KO -0.03%), Realty Income (O +1.18%), and Altria Group (MO +1.95%).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By James Brumley – Nov 26, 2026 at 9:31AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Coca-Cola ›.

    Sources indicate that will you need dividend income at some point in the future? For most people who plan on eventually retiring from the world of work, the answer is yes. They're growing their nest eggs in the meantime, in fact, largely with the intention of converting their growth investments into income investments when the time comes.

    That isn't necessarily the only way to meet your future income needs, though. As difficult as it may be to believe, there's an argument to be made for beginning to build your dividend-paying positions right now, even if you don't need the income yet.

    And while nobody can perfectly predict the future, your most promising dividend prospects for this purpose are Coca-Cola (KO -0.03%), Realty Income (O +1.18%), and Altria Group (MO +1.95%).

    Sources indicate that these names are among the market's most reliable and highest-yielding dividend payers, and each has raised its annualized dividend for at least 50 consecutive years, reflecting the resiliency of their underlying businesses. That makes all three of them Dividend Kings.

    Their dividend pedigrees aren't as vital as the process, however. How does one turn a $500 monthly investment in these names into a portfolio capable of producing more than $1,000 in monthly dividend income by, say, 20 years from now, in 2046?

    There are two stages to the process.

    The first is the growth phase. Rather than pocketing the dividends these stocks will be paying in the coming two decades, you'll be reinvesting these payments into more shares of the ticker while also purchasing more of these same stocks with your monthly contributions of $500.

    In a recent development, this is no minor growth driver. Over the past 20 years, dividend reinvestment has essentially doubled the effective net returns each of these stocks would have achieved with price appreciation alone.

    Industry observers note that the other aspect of the first stage is a bit trickier to get a handle on. That's figuring out the likely net returns these three names will achieve between now and 2046. Although past performance doesn't guarantee future results, experienced investors know that it's a pretty good indicator of what's likely to happen.

    Nevertheless, given the modest but steady traction the smoking-cessation movement is getting, it seems unlikely that tobacco giant Altria will deliver a repeat performance of the past two decades in the next two. For that matter, Coca-Cola's net gains since 2006 have also been exaggerated.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    So, for the sake of simplicity and plausibility, let's just assume all three of these stocks have and will continue to at least match the overall market's average annual net gain of 10%. (Each has beaten this figure, actually.) Investing $500 per month in any instruments achieving this sort of annual return for 20 years would leave you with a portfolio worth a little more than $380,000 at the end of this time frame.

    And again, just for the sake of simplicity, let's assume this $380,000 nest egg is evenly allocated between Altria, Realty Income, and Coca-Cola. Those are positions of roughly $127,000 each. How much dividend income would these collective investments be producing then?

    It has been revealed that we're still required to make some assumptions, albeit not unreasonable ones. Namely, let's assume these stocks' current dividend yields will more or less be their yields at that time. That's 2.2% for Coca-Cola, 5.6% for Realty Income, and 6% for Altria. Based on those numbers, this $380,000 in stock holdings should generate over $17,000 in dividends every year, or more than $1,400 in monthly spendable income.

    Sources indicate that just don't forget to turn your dividend reinvestment plan off when you're ready to start collecting these dividend payments in cash. That's the second stage of the process.

    These results are just hypothetical, of course, although the assumptions are rooted in real-world numbers that should be roughly repeatable.

    The substantial takeaway isn't identifying these three dividend payers as your top future income prospects, although there's little doubt that these companies will still be experiencing solid demand for their goods and services into the foreseeable future.

    In a recent development, no, the real takeaway is just how much even small regular investments in dividend stocks, paired with a dividend reinvestment plan, can grow your portfolio over time. This strategy can yield growth-like returns — the key is just giving it enough time to do the job. Note that most of the net growth for all three of these positions materialized in just the last one-third of the 20-year accumulation period.

    Recent findings suggest that the other related takeaway is that even though it may be years down the road for you, it wouldn't be wrong to start thinking about — and even building — positions in the dividend-paying stocks that you know you'll want to own as your income-generating positions then. Although dividends paid by stocks not held in retirement accounts are taxable as income for the year in which they're paid, that may still be a smarter option for you than buying growth investments that will result in large capital gains tax bills when you're ready to convert them into income-generating holdings.

    In a recent development, operator: Hello, ladies and gentlemen. Thank you for joining OMS Energy Technologies, Inc.'s Earnings Presentation for the first half of fiscal year 2027. Today's presentation is being recorded. The company's financial and operating results for the 6 months ended September 30, 2026, have been released and are available on the OMS Investor Relations website at ir.omsos.com.     According to recent reports, meng Hock How: Thank you, operator, and thank you to everyone joining us today. I am Meng Hock How, CEO of OMS Energy Technologies. I'll discuss our first half performance, what we're seeing in customer orders and the progress we're making across our business. I will then address several questions that we expect investors to have about the results. For investors newer to OMS, we are Singapore headquartered equipment manufacturer and engineered solutions supplier serving upstream oil and gas operators. Our core products include Surface Wellhead and Christmas Tree Systems, Specialty Connectors and Pipe. We also provide premium threading, repair, and other engineering services through 11 manufacturing facilities across 6 markets in Asia Pacific, Middle East, and North Africa. Turning to our results.

    I'm pleased to report that we expanded our gross margin, generated strong cash flow and further strengthened our debt-free balance sheet in the first half. Gross margin increased to 31.4% from 28.2% in the prior year period, and net profit margin improved to 18.8% from 17.6%. We generated $25.3 million in operating cash flow and approximately twice our net profit and ended September with a record $172.3 million in cash, cash equivalents, and restricted cash or approximately $4.06 per share. We delivered these results while macro conditions remain challenging given ongoing geopolitical uncertainty and supply chain disruption in our major markets. Our facilities remained operational throughout the period.

    Sources indicate that customers continued to tender and place orders with OMS during the half, but took longer to commit and schedule deliveries, weighing on revenue. First half revenue was $66.7 million compared with $82.8 million a year ago, largely due to the slower pace of Saudi Aramco call-off orders. This was partially offset by increased activity in Malaysia and Thailand, showing the value of our diversified footprint. In the current environment, the challenge for OMS lies not in lack of opportunities, but in reduced visibility, extended decision cycle and execution timing. You will see that pattern throughout this period's result.

    In a recent development, with order timing harder to predict, we are concentrating on factors that we can control, including careful management of inventory, costs, and customer deliveries. By keeping inventory, purchasing and costs in line with the orders we actually received, we were able to protect profitability and generate strong cash flow despite fluctuating order volumes. Saudi Arabia is where reduced visibility and order timing have affected us most. Revenue from Specialty Connectors and Pipe was $37.1 million compared with $51.1 million a year ago as the timing of the order placed under our long-term supply agreement with Saudi Aramco continued to slow. I would like to emphasize, as previously mentioned, that these are deferred orders, not lost orders.

    It has been revealed that our agreement with Saudi Aramco remains intact. Our relationship remains strong, and there has been no cancellation. To that end, we continue to receive business from Aramco. In September, we revealed a $7.1 million order for specialty connectors and pipe won through an open tender outside our long-term agreement. Since that award, we have received a call-off order of approximately $3 million under the long-term agreement as well as a separate $500,000 order for loose connectors for Aramco's float equipment. We view these awards as a reflection of Aramco's confidence in our product and the delivery record we have built in the Kingdom over 15 years.

    In Indonesia, our operation in Bogor just received an order for specialty pipe and connectors valued at approximately $396,000 for Pertamina North West Java. This is a follow-on from the order we unveiled in January 2026. Furthermore, our operations in Singapore and Malaysia secured their first order for specialty connectors and pipe for Petronas in Malaysia, valued at approximately $687,000. Of that amount, $367,000 was delivered during the first half of fiscal 2027. We also continue to bid for supply contracts with Kuwait Oil Company, KOC, and are actively engaged in the tender process we have entered after we qualified for the approved vendor list in July.

    According to recent reports, also following that qualification, we received a $458,000 order from Tenaris for OMS connectors that we welded onto Tenaris pipe and supplied to Kuwait Oil Tech giant as part of Tenaris OCTG package. While modest in size, the Petronas and Tenaris order extend our specialty connectors and pipe business to 2 more national oil companies, which we believe can lead to additional business over time. We've also recently bid to supply specialty connectors and Pipe for a development in the South China Sea with results expected next month. If we are successful, this will mark our reentry into China after more than 10 years and represent further progress in our ongoing geographic diversification efforts.

    In surface wellhead and Christmas trees, we continue to win orders while revenue follows customer and project schedules. First half revenue from Surface Wellhead and Christmas Tree was $3.5 million compared to $6.2 million a year ago. Indonesia is the main market for this business and upstream activities there has been slow over the past year as new oil and gas projects have taken longer to come online. In September, we declared $2.3 million order from Pertamina Hulu Rokan under our existing 3-year supply contract following the contract extension we announced in March. We also recently received $766,000 order from Pertamina for choke valves, a component of Christmas tree systems.

    It has been revealed that separately, we are awaiting a call-off of approximately $1 million from Pertamina under an existing contract. We also completed the stackup and function test of a newly introduced compact surface wellhead and Christmas tree system for Pertamina, a milestone in developing our wellhead product offering with an established customer. The equipment has been delivered and is being installed by Pertamina on its Tamadun-001 field, where it is carrying out an unconventional drilling program. Indonesia holds vast unconventional oil and gas resources, including shale gas, coal-bed methane, methane hydrate, and shale oil, and commercial development is still at an early stage. We believe this installation position us well as that activity develops.

    In a recent development, OMS Singapore has also just delivered a complete 10,000 psi wellhead and Christmas tree system to Orient Petroleum in Pakistan, marking OMS Singapore's first delivery of such a system to the country. Orient Petroleum is one of Pakistan's largest private exploration and production organization and has been operating since 1979. OMS Singapore has also received a supply contract for 2 sets of production tree for a Bleiswijk geothermal cluster in Netherlands. While the value is small at approximately $130,000, it is a step into the European energy sector that we want to build on. Across our service businesses, customers also continued to place orders during the half.

    Other ancillary services revenue rose to $9.4 million from $7.5 million, an increase of approximately 25%, supported by repair, refurbishment, and engineering work in Thailand and Malaysia. This maintenance work depends less on fresh project approval than equipment sales do. Premium threading services revenue was $16.7 million compared to $18 million. Together, our services business accounted for approximately 39% of first half revenue, up from approximately 31% a year ago. In Singapore, we've also secured an approximately $0.55 million of repair work on production risers for a large oilfield services company for the upcoming Kikeh 3B Phase 2 subsea project in Malaysia. The Kikeh field is operated by PTTEP Malaysia. Our backlog reflects the period's slower order timing pattern.

    At September 30, it stood at $40.9 million compared to $60.7 million at March 31, primarily due to call-off timing under the Saudi agreement. Our backlog comprises confirmed orders that have not yet been recognized as revenue and are expected to be delivered within the following 12 months. It does not include orders received after September 30, including the additional Saudi Aramco order I mentioned earlier. A framework agreement, a tender opportunity, and a confirmed call-off each represent different stages of the customer's procurement process and the backlog captures only the last of those stages. Today, opportunities are taking longer to move from tender to award and from framework agreement to call-off.

    To put the backlog figure in context, Saudi Aramco maintained its 2026 capital spending guidance of $50 billion to $55 billion when it reported third quarter's results this month. Aramco attributed lower upstream spending in the quarter, mainly to the timing of crude oil increment projects and several of its major upstream developments, including the Dammam development and the second phase of Jafurah are scheduled to come on stream in 2027. Across the wider region, BMI expects oil and gas capital spending to grow about 4% this year and to average approximately 6% a year from 2027 to 2030. Now let me walk through our financial results in more detail.

    In a recent development, first half revenue was $66.7 million compared to $82.8 million in the prior year period. Gross profit was $21 million compared to $23.3 million. Gross margin increased from 28.2% to 31.4%, supported by a more favorable mix in Saudi Specialty connectors and pipe and a greater contribution from higher-margin ancillary services in Thailand. Selling and general and administrative expenses were $7.1 million compared to $5.4 million in the prior year period. The increase primarily reflected personnel costs and professional services, governance, and compliance-related fees. Operating profit was $13.9 million compared to $17.9 million, and operating margin was 20.8% compared to 21.6%. Finance income increased to $2.4 million from $1.6 million, reflecting more cash placed in interest-earning deposits.

    It has been revealed that income tax expense was $3.6 million compared with $4.6 million, and our effective tax rate was 22.3% compared to 24%. Net profit was $12.6 million compared with $14.6 million, and net profit margin increased to 18.8% from 17.6%. Basic and diluted earnings per share were $0.28 compared with $0.33, reflecting lower profit attributable to shareholders and a higher weighted average share count. Adjusted EBITDA was $17.3 million compared to $21.8 million. Adjusted EBITDA margin held relatively steady at 25.9% compared with 26.4% despite the 19% decline in revenue. We continue to use this supplement measure alongside the IFRS results. The earnings release sets out the adjustment and the reconciliation from net profit. Cash generation remained an area of strength.

    Operating cash flow was $25.3 million compared with $26.4 million. Adjusted free cash flow was $19.9 million compared with $25.4 million. As described in our earnings release, this measure now deducts cash placed in fixed rate structured deposits, and the change from last year mainly reflects the $5 million we placed in these deposits during the period. Part of our cash generation came from a reduction in inventory, which contributed $9.5 million to operating cash flow compared to $12.2 million a year ago. Inventory ended September at $7.7 million compared to $17.2 million at March 31. The level of inventory and the timing of replenishment will affect cash flow as order activity changes.

    Industry observers note that we will continue to manage purchasing and production against the equipment needed for customer deliveries. Net cash used in investing activities was $5.4 million. This included $5 million placed in fixed rate structured deposits and approximately $0.4 million for property, plant, and equipment and software. These deposits are not included in our reported cash balance of $172.3 million. Cash and cash equivalents and restricted cash increased to a record $172.3 million at September 30 compared with $104.3 million at March 31. Our balance sheet remains free of bank borrowings. We continue to refine our capital allocation plan and assess investment opportunities while maintaining the financial flexibility to meet delivery commitments.

    Looking ahead, our immediate planning reflects the slow pace of Saudi call-off and the orders we have in hand across the business. The September Aramco tender win and the Pertamina order were announced with expected delivery dates in January and March 2027, respectively. We are focused on execution against the schedule and continued engagement with our customers. We remain cautious about the timing of a wider recovery in procurement. At the same time, we are encouraged by our recent order activity, the growing contribution from our services business and the opportunities we are pursuing across the Middle East and Asia.

    We have long-term agreement with leading national oil companies, 11 manufacturing facilities close to our customers and more than $172 million in cash with no debt. We believe this strength positions OMS well to capture future opportunities. Before we close, I would like to address questions investors are likely to have in the half, including how current visibility compares with the expectation that we discussed in June. Question one, how much of the earnings decline is attributable to geopolitical tensions and have projects been canceled? We have not observed material projects cancellation directly attributable to geopolitical development. The effect has been indirect primarily through longer customer decision cycle, deferred projects award and increased caution in customer capital spending decisions.

    For OMS, the main operating concern has been the slower pace of Saudi call-off orders. Some customers have taken longer to finalize investment decisions or have adjusted project time lines, and it is difficult to isolate a specific financial impact. Opportunities remain in place, but decision and awards are taking longer. We are actively pursuing work in Malaysia, Indonesia, the UAE, Kuwait and China. Question two, is demand weakening, particularly in the Middle East? We would characterize the environment as one of increased caution rather than broad-based demand weakness. Activity levels vary by customers and markets. Customers continue to evaluate opportunities and pursue strategic projects, although decision-making and approval processes have become more measured.

    It has been revealed that in certain cases, this has translated into longer approval and procurement cycles. For OMS, that reveals up as a slower Saudi call-off and a longer gap between tender and award. Several of the largest oilfield services have also pointed to the limited near-term visibility in the Middle East in their recent results. Even so, Saudi Aramco has maintained its 2026 capital spending guidance and has continued to award us business, including the $7.1 million tender award in September and additional orders since then. Our focus remains on supporting customers while adapting to changing market conditions. Third question, have supply chain disruption become a major concern? Supply chain conditions remain manageable, but less predictable than in previous period.

    We have experienced longer lead time and occasional logistic challenges affecting certain projects. Management continues to work closely with suppliers and customers to mitigate these impacts where possible. The fourth question, how are margins holding up? And can they be sustained? Well, first half gross margin increased to 31.4% from 28.2%, supported by the mix of equipment specification and services. Operating margin was 20.8%. We continue to manage procurement, project execution and operating costs carefully. Our priority is maintaining financial discipline while remaining competitive in the markets we serve. However, if activity slows further in the second half, margins could be affected. We will continue to manage costs carefully as conditions evolve.

    Recent findings suggest that question five, do we expect conditions to improve in the second half? Given the uncertain geopolitical and macroeconomic environment, we do not believe it will be appropriate to speculate on the timing or extent of any improvement. Customers continue to tender and place orders with OMS. Improvement depends on visibility returning and decision cycles shortening, and we do not control that timing. Continued uncertainty could further influence customer spending, project timing and supply chain performance. We continue to maintain long-standing customer relationships, technical capabilities and a diversified market presence. Management remains focused on factors within our control, including customer engagement, operational execution, cost management, and cash generation.

    Sixth question is, does the expectation of modest FY 2027 revenue growth discussed in June still hold? Well, in June, we expected fiscal 2027 revenue to be modestly above fiscal 2026, assuming no further material geopolitical disruption. Since then, the Saudi call-off activity has remained slow and the timing of a broader pickup remains uncertain. Given the first half revenue of $66.7 million and the continued slow pace of call-off, we no longer expect fiscal 2027 revenue to exceed fiscal 2026. We're not providing a specific range today, and we will patch investors as visibility on order timing improves. The last point or question 7, how do you proposal to use your cash?

    In a recent development, well, our priorities are consistent with what we shared in June. First, we are reinvesting in core businesses, including capacity, certification, and in-region capabilities that support our growth. Second, we continue to review bolt-on acquisition opportunities with discipline and our cash position allows us to pursue them without raising latest capital or taking on debt. We do not presently have a dividend and buyback program in place, but our balance sheet gives us the flexibility to introduce one when timing and conditions are right. We continue to refine our capital allocation initiative, and we'll update investors as it develops. With this, we conclude our prepared remarks. Thank you very much for joining us today.

    Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you all for participating. You may now disconnect your lines. Thank you.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Jennifer Saibil – Nov 26, 2026 at 10:13AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›.

    Recent findings suggest that anthropic (ANT +1.08%) made history last week when it went public in the largest initial public offering (IPO) ever. But so far, the stock isn't moving in the direction shareholders would hope for. The stock, which went public at $83 per share, opened its first day of trading at $111.50, and closed it at $97.17, has fallen to $77.40 as of this writing. That’s a 7% drop from the IPO price, and a much steeper one from the prices that retail investors could get on Day 1.

    But things can change promptly in the stock market, and a year from now, Anthropic could be much higher -- or much lower. Let's consider what a $5,000 investment in Anthropic stock might be worth in a year.

    The theory behind the bull case for Anthropic is that its Claude artificial intelligence (AI) model will be integrated into businesses everywhere. As of now, it already has 11,900 customers paying it at least $100,000 annually, including 250 customers with annual spending of more than $10 million. Widespread enterprise adoption of Claude could lead to a state where it's simply viewed as a necessary part of business operations; that would generate incredible growth at Anthropic.

    Sources indicate that the tech giant’s most recent results have been phenomenal. Trailing-12-month revenue increased 1,200% year over year in the third quarter, and if it continues to demonstrate such staggering growth, it could quickly become one of the largest companies in the world by sales. It would also become profitable at scale, and its vast investments in compute power — which it has been gobbling up from a roster of top AI infrastructure providers such as Amazon (AMZN -3.12%), Alphabet (GOOG -2.02%)(GOOGL -2.13%), and Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.30%)— would yield results. It has spending agreements with these companies and others to the tune of around $900 billion, with deals extending into 2036.

    Recent findings suggest that management sees vast use cases for its technology. It envisions AI helping to end poverty and cure disease as well as drive economic growth.

    It has been revealed that AI is definitely heating up, but it may not offer long-term growth in quite the way Anthropic imagines. To begin with, there are already many competitors offering foundation models, and as the technology changes, there could be more. The market is already forgetting how AI stocks tumbled when the Chinese-developed model Deepseek came onto the scene last year. There's no reason to believe other things like that can't happen. Anthropic itself is an extremely young company, and it only released Claude in 2023, pulling market share from OpenAI's ChatGPT.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    It has been revealed that IPO stocks tend to have bumpy rides early on, and given Anthropic's high price-to-sales multiple of 29, the stock has considerable room to drop if the company’s growth slows down. Wall Street expects its revenue to increase by 137% in 2027 — but that would be a major deceleration. If that forecast proves accurate, the market may conclude that Anthropic isn’t worth such a lofty sales multiple. If its top-line growth meets Wall Street's expectations, revenue would be about $83 billion. But if its P/S ratio gets cut in half to 14, its market cap would be $1.16 trillion. That's a 16% increase from today's value, turning a $5,000 investment made now into a position worth about $5,800.

    Latest Update: Rocket Lab Stock Just Fell to Its Lowest Price in About a Year. Is It a Buy Now?

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (826 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that rocket Lab (RKLB +2.26%) stock fell about 7% on Wednesday, Nov.
    • The growth stock had closed above $66 just two weeks before, soon after Rocket Lab's third-quarter results, and about a third of that value has vanished since.
    • But the business behind the stock is far bigger than it was the last time shares traded this low.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Daniel Sparks – Nov 26, 2026 at 10:23AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Rocket Lab ›.

    Industry observers note that rocket Lab (RKLB +2.26%) stock fell about 7% on Wednesday, Nov. 25, to roughly $43 as I write. The drop left shares at their lowest price since early December 2025 and over 70% below their May 27 record close of $150.23.

    The growth stock had closed above $66 just two weeks before, soon after Rocket Lab's third-quarter results, and about a third of that value has vanished since.

    But the business behind the stock is far bigger than it was the last time shares traded this low. What hasn't changed is that Neutron, the reusable rocket behind Rocket Lab's long-term growth looks, hasn't yet flown.

    The last time Rocket Lab stock traded this low, in early December 2025, the company's revenue for the previous four quarters came to around $555 million. For the last four quarters, it's about $882 million, almost 60% more. Growth has sped up, too. Revenue for the third quarter of 2026 climbed 73% from a year earlier to a record $268 million, after growing 36% in the fourth quarter of 2025. And management expects fourth-quarter revenue of $270 million to $290 million, which at the midpoint would be 56% above the year-ago quarter -- still fast, though slower than the third quarter's rate.

    Industry observers note that the share count grew, too, but far more slowly. Rocket Lab sold around $3.9 billion in newly introduced stock through September, partly to pay for its pending purchase of satellite operator Iridium Communications. Counting preferred stock that converts to common shares, it had about 15% more shares at the end of September than at the end of 2025.

    Industry observers note that that leaves much more revenue behind each share. At roughly $43, Rocket Lab is valued at about $29 billion, which comes to 33 times the revenue it took in over the last year. At the same share price in early December 2025, the stock traded at more than 40 times sales.

    Still, 33 times sales is a high valuation for a business that isn't profitable yet, and I think much of that price depends on Neutron.

    Rocket Lab now has 16 Neutron missions booked before the rocket's first flight, and half of them were signed in the third quarter alone, for over $515 million.

    But at least six of those eight fresh missions aren't scheduled until late 2028 or later. Radar-satellite firm ICEYE's three rolls out start in late 2028, Muon Space's two are set for 2029 and 2030, and Starcloud's is booked for 2029.

    Rocket Lab expects only around a third of its $3.6 billion total backlog (signed work it hasn't yet counted as revenue) to become revenue within 12 months. Neutron's far-off missions likely make up a big part of the rest.

    Sources indicate that neutron's first launch, meanwhile, is expected in 2027. Before Rocket Lab picks a specific date, it still needs to put together the rocket's first-stage tank and finish pressure and cryogenic (super-cold) testing, according to its last quarterly report.

    Neutron has to fly first, and even then its early missions might not make money. In the third quarter, Rocket Lab recorded a forward loss reserve (an expected loss booked ahead of time) on the vehicle for Neutron's second flight, because the rocket is still so early in development.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

    Until Neutron flies regularly, the losses will likely keep coming. Rocket Lab lost $18 million in the third quarter on a non-GAAP (adjusted) basis, measured by earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA). That was smaller than its $26 million loss a year earlier, and management expects another loss of $14 million to $20 million in the fourth quarter.

    On the third-quarter earnings call, CFO Adam Spice stated capital spending should stay high as Neutron heads toward production, but he expects adjusted EBITDA to go positive within six months of the rocket's first successful test flight.

    In a recent development, I think it can be, for investors willing to wait for Neutron. Each share now comes with much more revenue than it did at this price a year ago, and customers keep booking Neutron releases. But Neutron still has to show it can fly, then fly often. And a stock that shed a third of its value over two weeks might swing just as hard again. I'd consider buying in stages instead of all at once.
